Define $t_{\pm}$ as in (\ref{eq:tpm}). It follows from the $r$-equation
(\ref{eq:RPertEqn}), Corollary \ref{cor:YoungPertEst}, the estimates
(\ref{eq:LightLength}) and (\ref{eq:NegCosPertPf}) that 

\begin{align*}
2m_{0}a_{0} & =r_{t_{+}}-r_{t_{-}}=\int_{t_{-}}^{t_{+}}dr_{s}\\
 & =\int_{t_{-}}^{t_{+}}A(X_{s})dw_{s}+\int_{t_{-}}^{t_{+}}\cos(r_{s}+\alpha_{s}-\phi_{s})|\dot{h}_{s}|ds\\
 & \leqslant K\Xi_{I}+\mu_{h}(E)\leqslant K\eta_{0}+m_{0}a_{0}.
\end{align*}
By requiring $\eta_0$ to satisfy
\begin{equation}
K\eta_{0}<m_{0}a_{0},\label{eq:Eta02}
\end{equation}
one reaches a contradiction. 

To summarise, one first chooses $\eta_{0}$ that satisfies (\ref{eq:Eta01},
\ref{eq:Eta02}) and then chooses $A_{0}$ to satisfy (\ref{eq:A0}).
With such choices, for any $(I,a;w,h)$ satisfying the conditions
(\ref{eq:WHAs1}, \ref{eq:WHAs2}, \ref{eq:WHAs3}), the interval
$I$ must contain an $(a_{0},\theta_{0})$-effective turn of $h$.
This completes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
We continue to use the same notation as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:NonPertCoer}
(the annuli decomposition $[a_{j},b_{j}]$ and radial crossing $I_{j}=[s_{j},t_{j}]$).
Let $R>2A_{0}$ ($A_{0}$ is the constant appearing in Lemma \ref{lem:ILengthPert}
so that $a_{j}>A_{0}$ for every $j$). Our goal is to estimate the
number of $I_{j}$'s which do not contain an $(a_{0},\theta_{0})$-effective
turn of $h$. According to Lemma \ref{lem:ILengthPert}, at least
one of the constraints in (\ref{eq:WHAs2}, \ref{eq:WHAs3}) fails
for such $I_{j}$'s. We discuss the possibilities as follows.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) \uline{\mbox{$\omega_{I_{j}}>\delta$}.} 

\vspace{2mm} Since $\|w\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M$, one has 
\[
\delta^{p}\cdot\big|\{j:\omega_{I_{j}}>\delta\}\big|\leqslant\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}^{p}\leqslant M^{p}.
\]
As a result, 
\begin{equation}
\big|\{j:\omega_{I_{j}}>\delta\}\big|\leqslant\delta^{-p}M^{p}.\label{eq:C1}
\end{equation}
(ii) \uline{\mbox{$l_{I_{j}}>\gamma_{0}a_{j}/2$}.}

\vspace{2mm} Since $a_{j}\geqslant R/2$, one has 
\[
\frac{\gamma_{0}R}{4}\cdot\big|\{j:l_{I_{j}}>\gamma_{0}a_{j}/2\}\big|\leqslant\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}l_{I_{j}}\leqslant\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}.
\]
Therefore, 
\begin{equation}
\big|\{j:l_{I_{j}}>\gamma_{0}a_{j}/2\}\big|\leqslant\frac{4\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}}{\gamma_{0}R}.\label{eq:C2}
\end{equation}
(iii) \uline{\mbox{$\Xi_{I_{j}}>\eta_{0}$}.} 

\vspace{2mm} By definition, one has 
\begin{equation}
\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\Xi_{I_{j}}\leqslant\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}l_{I_{j}}^{\theta}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}^{1+\theta}.\label{eq:SumXi}
\end{equation}
The first sum in (\ref{eq:SumXi}) is estimated as 
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}\leqslant N_{R}^{1-1/p}\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}^{p}\Big)^{1/p}\leqslant MN_{R}^{1-1/p}.
\]
For the second sum in (\ref{eq:SumXi}), one can first use H\"older's
inequality to obtain that 
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}l_{I_{j}}^{\theta}\leqslant M\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}l_{I_{j}}^{\theta p'}\Big)^{1/p'}.
\]
Next, observe that $\theta p'>1$. Since the $l^{p}$-norm is nonincreasing
in $p$, one has 
\[
\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}l_{I_{j}}^{\theta p'}\Big)^{1/p'}\leqslant\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}l_{I_{j}}\Big)^{\theta}\leqslant\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}^{\theta}.
\]
As a consequence, 
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}l_{I_{j}}^{\theta}\leqslant M\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}^{\theta}.
\]
The last sum in (\ref{eq:SumXi}) again easily estimated by monotonicity
of $l^{p}$-norm; since $1+\theta>p$, one has 
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}^{1+\theta}\leqslant\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}^{p}\Big)^{\frac{1+\theta}{p}}\leqslant M^{1+\theta}.
\]
To summarise, one concludes that 
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\Xi_{I_{j}}\leqslant M\Big(\frac{R}{6\pi}\Big)^{1-1/p}+M\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}^{\theta}+M^{1+\theta}.
\]
It follows that 
\begin{equation}
\big|\{j:\Xi_{I_{j}}>\eta_{0}\}\big|\leqslant\eta_{0}^{-1}\Big[M\Big(\frac{R}{6\pi}\Big)^{1-1/p}+M\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}^{\theta}+M^{1+\theta}\Big].\label{eq:C3}
\end{equation}
The number of $j$'s such that $I_{j}$ does not contain an $(a_{0},\theta_{0})$-effective
turn is therefore bounded above by the sum of the RHS of (\ref{eq:C1},
\ref{eq:C2}, \ref{eq:C3}). Since $N_{R}=\frac{R}{6\pi}$, this immediately
yields a lower bound of ${\cal N}_{{\rm eff}}(h)$ in the form of
(\ref{eq:TurnEstPert}). The proof of Lemma \ref{lem:TurnEstPert}
is now complete.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Let $({\cal W},\bar{{\cal H}},\mu)$ be the abstract Wiener space
associated with the 2D fBM (in particular, $\mu$ is the law of fBM).
Fix $p\in(1/H)^{+}$ as before and fix $M>0$ (its precise value is
of no importance). Define
\[
G_{M}:=\big\{ w\in{\cal W}:\|w\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M\big\}.
\]
For each $R>0,$ we also set 
\[
A_{R}:=\Big\{ w\in{\cal W}:\sup_{0\leqslant t\leqslant1}|X_{t}^{w}|>R\Big\}
\]
According to Proposition \ref{prop:KeyCoer}, there exist positive
constants $c_{0},R_{0},$ such that 
\[
G_{M}+c_{0}R^{H+1/2}{\cal K}\subseteq A_{R}^{c}
\]
for all $R>R_{0},$ where ${\cal K}$ denotes the closed unit ball
of $\bar{{\cal H}}.$ Let 
\[
\kappa:=\Phi^{-1}(\mu(G_{M}))\in\mathbb{R},
\]
where $\Phi(u):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{x}e^{-u^{2}/2}du$.
It follows from Borell's isoperimetric inequality (see \cite[Theorem 4.3]{Led94})
that 
\begin{align*}
\mu(A_{R}) & =1-\mu(A_{R}^{c})\leqslant1-\mu\big(G_{M}+c_{0}R^{H+1/2}{\cal K}\big)\\
 & \leqslant1-\Phi(\kappa+c_{0}R^{H+1/2})\leqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^{2H+1}}
\end{align*}
for all $R>R_{0}$ with suitable constants $C_{1},C_{2}>0.$ This
completes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:2DCounter}.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- rem-9: body_md -->
Geometrically, Condition (H) asserts that level sets of the function $F$ are uniformly transversal to integral curves of the vector field $W_\eta$.
<!-- end rem-9 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:GLowH}Let $H\in(1/2,1)$ and $V_0,V_1,\cdots,V_d\in C_b^2$. Suppose that Condition (H) holds. Then there exist
positive constants $C_{1},C_{2}$ depending only on $H$ and the vector fields, such that
the estimate
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(\big|X_{1}-x_{0}\big|>R\big)\geqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^{2}}
\]
holds for all large $R$.
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
As usual, we use $X_{t}^{w}$ to denote the solution to the same equation
(\ref{eq:SDEIntro}) with $B_{t}$ replaced by $w_{t}$. Given $R>0,$
we set $h_{t}^{R}:=Rt\eta$ ($0\leqslant t\leqslant1$) where $\eta$
is the unit vector given by Condition (H). This particular Cameron-Martin
path will play a critical role in the argument. Let $F$ be the function
given by Condition (H).

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) The key claim is that there exist positive
constants $M,C_{0},R_{0}$ depending only on $p,H,V,F$, such that
\begin{equation}
\|w\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M\implies\big|X_{1}^{w+h^{R}}-x\big|\geqslant C_{0}R\label{eq:DispEstYoung}
\end{equation}
for all $R>R_{0}.$ 

To prove this claim, let us write $X_{t}:=X_{t}^{w+h^{R}}$ and $V=(V_{1},\cdots,V_{d})$
for simplicity. Note that $X_{t}$ satisfies the following equation:
\[
dX_{t}=RW_{\eta}(X_{t})dt+V(X_{t})dw_{t}+V_{0}(X_{t})dt.
\]
Let $F$ be the function given by Condition (H). By applying the chain
rule to $F(X_{t})$, one obtains that 
\begin{align*}
F(X_{1})-F(x_{0})= & R\int_{0}^{1}(W_{\eta}F)(X_{t})dt+\int_{0}^{1}\big(\nabla F(X_{t})\big)^{T}V(X_{t})dw_{t}\\
 & \ \ \ +\int_{0}^{1}\big(\nabla F(X_{t})\big)^{T}V_{0}(X_{t})dt=:A+B+C.
\end{align*}
According to Condition (H), one has $A\geqslant mR$. It is also obvious
that $|C|\leqslant\|DF\|_{\infty}\|V_{0}\|_{\infty}.$ 

To estimate $B$, let us set 
\[
x_{I}:=\|X\|_{p\text{-var};I},\quad\omega_{I}:=\|\omega\|_{p\text{-var};I}
\]
for any given interval $I\subseteq[0,1]$. By using \cite[Theorem 6.8]{FV10},
one easily finds that 
\[
x_{I}\leqslant\big(R\|V\|_{\infty}+\|V_{0}\|_{\infty}\big)|I|+C_{p}\big(\|V\|_{\infty}+\|DV\|_{\infty}x_{I}\big)\omega_{I}.
\]
Let $M$ be chosen such that 
\[
C_{p}\|DV\|_{\infty}M<\frac{1}{2}.
\]
Whenever $\|w\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M$, one has 
\begin{equation}
x_{I}\leqslant2\big(R\|V\|_{\infty}+\|V_{0}\|_{\infty}\big)|I|+2C_{p}\|V\|_{\infty}M.\label{eq:xIEst}
\end{equation}
Now we divide the interval $[0,1]$ into equal subintervals $I_{1},\cdots,I_{N}$
($N\asymp R$) each having length $1/R$. According to (\ref{eq:xIEst}),
on each subinterval $I_{j}$ one has 
\begin{equation}
x_{I_{j}}\leqslant C_{p,V}\label{eq:xIjEst}
\end{equation}
with some constant $C_{p,V}$ depending on $p,V.$ It follows
again from \cite[Theorem 6.8]{FV10} and (\ref{eq:xIjEst}) that 
\begin{align*}
|B| & \leqslant\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Big|\int_{I_{j}}\big(\nabla F(X_{t})\big)^{T}V(X_{t})dw_{t}\Big|\\
 & \leqslant C_{p}\big(\|(\nabla F)^{T}\cdot V\|_{\infty}+C_{p,V}\big\|D\big((\nabla F)^{T}\cdot V\big)\big\|_\infty\big)\sum_{j=1}^{N}\omega_{I_{i}}\\
 & \leqslant C'_{p,V,F}R^{1-1/p}\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N}\omega_{I_{j}}^{p}\Big)^{1/p}\\
 & \leqslant C'_{p,V,F}MR^{1-1/p}.
\end{align*}
As a consequence, 
\begin{align*}
\|\nabla F\|_{\infty}|X_{1}-x_{0}| & \geqslant F(X_{1})-F(x_{0})\\
 & \geqslant mR-C'_{p,V,F}MR^{1-1/p}-\|DF\|_{\infty}\|V_{0}\|_{\infty}.
\end{align*}
Let $R_{0}$ be chosen such that the RHS is larger than $mR/2$ for
all $R>R_{0}.$ The claim (\ref{eq:DispEstYoung}) thus follows with
$C_{0}:=\frac{m}{2\|\nabla F\|_{\infty}}.$

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) The claim (\ref{eq:DispEstYoung}) shows
that 
\[
G_{M}:=\big\{ w:\|w\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M\big\}\subseteq\Big\{\big|X_{1}^{w+h^{R}}-x_{0}\big|\geqslant C_{0}R\Big\}
\]
for all $R>R_{0}.$ As a consequence, 
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(\big|X_{1}^{B}-x_{0}\big|\geqslant C_{0}R\big)\geqslant\mu(h^{R}+G_{M}),
\]
where $\mu$ is the law of fBM on path space. By exactly the same
Cameron-Martin transformation argument as in the proof of Theorem
\ref{thm:RoughLowG}, one finds that 
\[
\mu(h^{R}+G_{M})=e^{-\|h^{R}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}^{2}/2}\mathbb{E}\big[e^{-\int_{0}^{1}\langle\theta_{t}^{R},dW_{t}\rangle}{\bf 1}_{G_{M}}(B)\big].
\]
Here $\theta^{R}:=K_{H}^{-1}h^{R}\in L^{2}([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{d})$
($K_{H}$ is the isomorphism defined by (\ref{eq:KHIso})) and $W$
is the Wiener process in the fBM representation (\ref{eq:fBMRep}).
By the definition of $h^{R},$ it is obvious that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hRNorm}
\|h^{R}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}=R\|[t\mapsto t\eta]\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}=:\kappa R.
\end{equation}
In addition, due to the reflection symmetry of the set $G_{M}$, one
has 
\[
\mathbb{E}\big[e^{-\int_{0}^{1}\langle\theta_{t}^{R},dW_{t}\rangle}{\bf 1}_{G_{M}}(B)\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\int_{0}^{1}\langle\theta_{t}^{R},dW_{t}\rangle}{\bf 1}_{G_{M}}(B)\big].
\]
In particular, 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\big[e^{-\int_{0}^{1}\langle\theta_{t}^{R},dW_{t}\rangle}{\bf 1}_{G_{M}}(B)\big] & =\mathbb{E}\Big[\cosh\Big(\int_{0}^{1}\langle\theta_{t}^{R},dW_{t}\rangle\Big){\bf 1}_{G_{M}}(B)\Big]\\
 & \geqslant\mu(G_{M}):=\delta.
\end{align*}
As a result, one concludes that 
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(\big|X_{1}^{B}-x_{0}\big|\geqslant C_{0}R\big)\geqslant\delta e^{-\kappa^{2}R^{2}/2}
\]
for all $R>R_{0}$. 

Now the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:GLowH} is complete.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- thm-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:GenLowYoung}
Consider the SDE (\ref{eq:SDEIntro}) with $H\in(1/2,1).$ Suppose that
the vector fields are $C_{b}^{\infty}$ and uniformly elliptic. Then
there exist positive constants $C_{1},C_{2}$ depending only on $H$
and the vector fields, such that the estimate 
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}\big(|X_{1}-x_{0}|>R\big)\geqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^{2H+1}}\label{eq:WeibullGenYoung}
\end{equation}
holds for all large $R$.
<!-- end thm-8 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
The argument is a simple adaptation of the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:GLowH}.
It is more convenient to use H\"older norms here. Fix a unit vector
$\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ and $\rho\in(1/2,H)$. Given $R>1$, let
$X_{t}^{R}$ denote the solution to the differential equation 
\[
dX_{t}^{R}=R\eta dt+V(X_{t}^{R})dB_{t}+V_{0}(X_{t}^{R})dt,\quad X_{0}^{R}=x_{0}.
\]
Similar to Part (i) of the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:GLowH} with
$p$-variation replaced by $\rho$-H\"older norm (cf. Lemma \ref{lem:LinDisplace}),
there exist positive constants $M,C_{1},C_{2},R_{0},$ such that on
the event 
\[
A_{M}:=\big\{\|B\|_{\rho\text{-H\"ol};[0,1]}\leqslant M\big\},
\]
the estimates
\begin{equation}
\big|X_{t}^{R}-X_{s}^{R}\big|\leqslant C_{1}\big(R|t-s|+M|t-s|^{\rho}+|t-s|\big)\label{eq:CtyEstGenLowYoung}
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation}
|X_{1}^{R,w}-x_{0}|\geqslant C_{2}R\label{eq:GloDispGenYoung}
\end{equation}
hold for all $R>R_{0}$ and $s,t\in[0,1]$. 

Now let us define the (random) Cameron-Martin path
\[
h_{t}^{R}:=R\int_{0}^{t}a(X_{s}^{R})ds,
\]
where $a(x):=A(x)\eta$ and $A(x)$ is the right inverse of $V(x)$
defined by (\ref{eq:RightInv}). Note that $h^{R}$ is ${\cal F}^{W}$-adapted
(cf. (\ref{eq:fBMRep})). According to the norm-equivalence relation
(\ref{eq:EquivFracNorm}), one has 
\begin{align*}
\|h^{R}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}^{2} & \leqslant C_{H}\Big(\|\dot{h}^{R}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{|\dot{h}_{t}^{R}-\dot{h}_{s}^{R}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{2H}}dsdt\Big)\\
 & =C_{H}R^{2}\Big(\|u^{R}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{|\dot{u}_{t}^{R}-\dot{u}_{s}^{R}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{2H}}dsdt\Big)
\end{align*}
where $u_{t}^{R}:=a(X_{t}^{R})$. The $L^{2}$-norm in the first term
is uniformly bounded by $\|A\|_{\infty}$. For the second term, by
using (\ref{eq:CtyEstGenLowYoung}) one easily finds that 
\[
\big|u_{t}^{R}-u_{s}^{R}\big|\leqslant C_{3}\big(\min\{1,R|t-s|\}+M|t-s|^{\rho}\big)
\]
for all $R>R_{0}$ and $s,t\in[0,1]$. It follows from explicit analysis
that 
\begin{align*}
 & \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{|\dot{u}_{t}^{R}-\dot{u}_{s}^{R}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{2H}}dsdt\\
 & \leqslant C_{3}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\Big(\frac{\min\{1,R^{2}|t-s|^{2}\}}{|t-s|^{2H}}+M|t-s|^{2\rho-2H}\Big)\\
 & \leqslant C_{4}R^{2H-1}
\end{align*}
on the event $A_{M}.$ As a consequence, 
\begin{equation}
\|h^{R}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}^{2}\leqslant C_{H}R^{2}\big(\|A\|_{\infty}^{2}+C_{4}R^{2H-1}\big)\leqslant C_{5}R^{2H+1}\label{eq:CMGenYoung}
\end{equation}
on $A_{M}.$

Let \[\tau:=\inf\big\{t\geqslant 0:\|B\|_{\rho\text{-H\"ol};[0,t]}>M\big\}\wedge 1\] and define 
\[\hat{h}^R_t := R\int_{0}^{t\wedge \tau}a(X_{s}^{R})ds.\]Note that $\hat{h}^R$ is also $\mathcal{F}^W$-adapted and $\hat{h}^R = h^R$ on $A_M$. From the above analysis, it is not hard to see that with probability one, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:CMGenYoung}
\big\|\dot{\hat{h}}^R\big\|_{\bar{\cal H}}\leqslant C_6 R^{2H+1}
\end{equation}for all $R$. With the global Cameron-Martin estimate (\ref{eq:CMGenYoung}), one can now carry through the Cameron-Martin transformation argument as in the
proof of Theorem \ref{thm:GLowH} (cf. the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:RoughLowG}) to conclude the desired $(2H+1)$-Weibull
lower bound (\ref{eq:WeibullGenYoung}).
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- thm-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:2DPeriodic}Let $V_{1},V_{2}$ be given smooth vector fields
on the torus $\mathbb{T}^{2}=\mathbb{R}^{2}/\mathbb{Z}^{2}.$ Suppose
that they are uniformly elliptic, namely, 
\[
\dim{\rm Span}\{V_{1}(x),V_{2}(x)\}=2
\]
for every $x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}$. Consider the SDE 
\begin{equation}
dX_{t}=\tilde{V}_{1}(X_{t})dB_{t}^{1}+\tilde{V}_{2}(X_{t})dB_{t}^{2},\quad X_{0}=x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\label{eq:SDETorus}
\end{equation}
on the universal cover $\mathbb{R}^{2}.$ Here $\tilde{V}_{i}$ is
the canonical periodic lifting of $V_{i}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and
$B_{t}=(B_{t}^{1},B_{t}^{2})$ is an fBM with Hurst parameter $H\in(1/2,1)$.
Then there exist positive constants $C_{1},C_{2}$, such that 
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}\big(|X_{1}-x_{0}|>R\big)\geqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^2}\label{eq:GaussLowTorus}
\end{equation}
for all large $R.$
<!-- end thm-9 -->
<!-- defn-5: body_md -->
\label{def:Folia}
Let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional differentiable manifold. Let ${\cal F}$
be a collection of immersed $k$-dimensional submanifolds. A chart
$(U,\varphi)$ is said to be \textit{flat} for ${\cal F}$ if the
following two properties hold:

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) $\varphi(U)$ is a cube in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$;

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) for each submanifold $N\in{\cal F}$ with
nonempty intersection with $U$, the set $\varphi(N\cap U)$ is a
countable union of $k$-dimensional slices of the form 
\[
x^{k+1}=c^{k+1},\cdots,x^{n}=c^{n}
\]
in $\varphi(U).$ 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent A \textit{$k$-dimensional (smooth) foliation}
on $M$ is a collection ${\cal F}$ of disjoint, connected, immersed
$k$-dimensional submanifolds such that the union of members of ${\cal F}$
is $M$ and for every $x\in M$, there exists a chart around $x$
which is flat for ${\cal F}.$ Members of a foliation ${\cal F}$
are called \textit{leaves} of ${\cal F}.$
<!-- end defn-5 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Let $M$ be a closed surface. Let $W$ be a smooth vector field on
$M$ which is everywhere nonvanishing. According to the global Frobenius
theorem, the integral curves of $W$ form a one-dimensional (1D) foliation
on $M$ (see \cite[Theorem 19.21]{Lee13}). This is the main example
that is relevant to us.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- defn-6: body_md -->
\label{def:Reeb}

Let ${\cal F}$ be a 1D foliation on $\mathbb{T}^{2}.$ We say that
${\cal F}$ \textit{has a Reeb component} if there exists an embedded
annulus $A\cong S^{1}\times[0,1]$ inside $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ such that:

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) $\partial A$ is the union of two compact
leaves of ${\cal F}$ that are in opposite homotopy classes;

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) there are no compact leaves of ${\cal F}$
in the interior of $A$.
<!-- end defn-6 -->
<!-- defn-7: body_md -->
\label{def:SuspensionMain}The foliation $(\Sigma_{f},{\cal F}_{f})$
is called the \textit{suspension} of the diffeomorphism $f$.
<!-- end defn-7 -->
<!-- defn-8: body_md -->
\label{def:Conj}

Let ${\cal F},{\cal F}'$ be $k$-dimensional foliations on $n$-dimensional
manifolds $M,M'$ respectively. We say that ${\cal F}$ and ${\cal F}'$
are \textit{conjugate} (or \textit{isomorphic}) if there exists a
diffeomorphism $\Psi:M\rightarrow M'$ such that $\Psi({\cal F})={\cal F}'$.
<!-- end defn-8 -->
<!-- thm-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:1DFoliClass}Let ${\cal F}$ be a 1D foliation on $\mathbb{T}^{2}$.
Then either ${\cal F}$ has a Reeb component or it is conjugate to
the suspension of an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:S^{1}\rightarrow S^{1}$.
<!-- end thm-10 -->
<!-- defn-9: body_md -->
For each $x\in\mathbb{T}^{2},$ the set $\{\phi_{t}(x):t\in\mathbb{R}\}$
is called the \textit{orbit} of $W$ through $x$. An orbit $\gamma$
is said to be \textit{periodic} if there exist $T>0$ and $x\in\gamma$
(equivalently, for all $x\in\gamma$) such that $\phi_{T}(x)=x$.
The smallest positive number satisfying the above relation is called
the \textit{period} of $\gamma$. A periodic orbit is \textit{noncontractible}
if its homology class in $H_{1}(\mathbb{T}^{2};\mathbb{Z})$ is nonzero.
<!-- end defn-9 -->
<!-- defn-10: body_md -->
The map $P$ constructed above is known as the \textit{Poincar\'e
map} at $x\in\gamma$ with respect to the transversal $\Sigma$.
The number $\lambda_{\gamma}$ is called the \textit{transverse characteristic
number} of $\gamma.$
<!-- end defn-10 -->
<!-- defn-11: body_md -->
\label{def:HypOrb}Let $\gamma$ be a periodic orbit of a smooth,
everywhere nonvanishing vector field $W$ on $\mathbb{T}^{2}$. We
say that $\gamma$ is \textit{hyperbolic} if $\lambda_{\gamma}\neq1$.
<!-- end defn-11 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
We
therefore assume that there exists a diffeomorphism $\Psi:\mathbb{T}^{2}\rightarrow\Sigma_{f}$,
where $\Sigma_{f}$ is the suspension of an orientation-preserving
diffeomorphism $f:S^{1}\rightarrow S^{1},$ such that $\Psi({\cal F}_{\alpha_{0}})={\cal F}_{f}$
(see Definition \ref{def:Suspension} and Definition \ref{def:Conj}). 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) Consider the projection 
\[
\rho:\Sigma_{f}\rightarrow S^{1}=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z},\quad\rho([x,t])\mapsto t\ \ ({\rm mod}\ \mathbb{Z}).
\]
Let $d\theta$ denote the canonical volume form on $S^{1}$ such that
$\int_{S^{1}}d\theta=1$. Define the closed $1$-form $\beta:=\rho^{*}(d\theta)$
on $\Sigma_{f}.$ Let $Y$ be the suspension vector field on $\Sigma_{f}$;
the vertical vector field $\partial_{t}$ on $S^{1}\times\mathbb{R}$
descends to $Y$ on $\Sigma_{f}$ under the quotient of the $\mathbb{Z}$-action
(\ref{eq:ZActSusp}), which is tangential to the foliation ${\cal F}_{f}$.
By definition, one has 
\[
\langle\beta(\xi),Y(\xi)\rangle=\langle d\theta,(d\rho)(Y)\rangle_{\rho(\xi)}=\langle d\theta,\partial_{t}\rangle_{\rho(\xi)}=1
\]
for every $\xi\in\Sigma_{f}$.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) Since $\Psi({\cal F}_{\alpha_{0}})={\cal F}_{f}$,
there exists a nonvanishing function $\lambda\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$
such that
\[
(d\Psi)_{x}(W_{\alpha_{0}}(x))=\lambda(x)Y(\Psi(x))
\]
for every $x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}.$ By connectedness, one may assume without loss of generality that 
\[
m:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}}\lambda(x)>0.
\]
Let $\eta:=\Psi^{*}(\beta).$ It follows that $\eta$ is closed and
one has 
\[
\langle\eta(x),W_{\alpha_{0}}(x)\rangle=\lambda(x)\langle\beta(\Psi(x)),Y(\Psi(x))\rangle=\lambda(x)
\]
for every $x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}.$ In particular, 
\begin{equation}
\inf_{x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}}\langle\eta(x),W_{\alpha_{0}}(x)\rangle=m>0.\label{eq:NonDegEta}
\end{equation}
(iii) We claim that the (de Rham) cohomology class $[\eta]$ is nontrivial.
Indeed, if $\eta$ were exact, say $\eta=dq$ for some $q\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$,
one would have $\eta(x^{*})=0$ at the location $x^{*}$ where $q$
is maximised. This contradicts the fact (\ref{eq:NonDegEta}). Therefore,
$[\eta]\neq0.$

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iv) Let $[\alpha_{1}],[\alpha_{2}]$ denote
a basis of $H_{1}(\Sigma_{f};\mathbb{Z})$ such that 
\begin{equation}
\int_{[\alpha_{1}]}[\beta]=0,\quad\int_{[\alpha_{2}]}[\beta]=1.\label{eq:BetaBasis}
\end{equation}
One can construct them in the following way. The loop $\alpha_{1}=([x,t])_{x\in S^{1}}$
is a circle positively winding around the horizontal $S^{1}$-component
once. The loop $\alpha_{2}$ is defined by a vertical curve $\alpha_{2}':=[(x,t)]_{0\leqslant t\leqslant1}$
concatenated with a horizontal arc $\alpha_{2}''$ joining $[(f(x),0)]$
back to $[(x,0)]$ along the horizontal $S^{1}$-component. This concatenation
is needed since $\alpha_{2}'$ may fail to be a closed curve (leaves
of ${\cal F}_{f}$ needs not be compact). The relation (\ref{eq:BetaBasis})
is now obvious from the construction. 

Let $\{[l_{1}],[l_{2}]\}$ be the canonical basis of $H_{1}(\mathbb{T}^{2};\mathbb{Z})$
that is dual to $\{[dx^{1}],[dx^{2}]\}$. Let $\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2}$
be the preimages of $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}$ under the diffeomorphism
$\Psi$. Then $\{[\zeta_{1}],[\zeta_{2}]\}$ is a basis of $H_{1}(\mathbb{T}^{2};\mathbb{Z})$
and one has 
\[
\int_{[\zeta_{1}]}[\eta]=0,\quad\int_{[\zeta_{2}]}[\eta]=1.
\]
In particular, one can write 
\[
[\zeta_{1}]=a[l_{1}]+b[l_{2}],\quad[\zeta_{2}]=c[l_{1}]+d[l_{2}]
\]
with some matrix 
\[
A=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
a & b\\
c & d
\end{array}\right)\in{\rm GL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z}).
\]
It follows that 
\[
[\eta]=k_{1}[dx^{1}]+k_{2}[dx^{2}],
\]
where 
\[
\left(\begin{array}{c}
k_{1}\\
k_{2}
\end{array}\right):=A^{-1}\cdot\left(\begin{array}{c}
0\\
1
\end{array}\right)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\backslash\{(0,0)\}.
\]
As a result, one has
\[
\eta=k_{1}dx^{1}+k_{2}dx^{2}+d\varphi
\]
for some $\varphi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2}).$

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (v) Consider the function 
\[
F(x^{1},x^{2}):=k_{1}x^{1}+k_{2}x^{2}+\tilde{\varphi}(x^{1},x^{2}),\quad x=(x^{1},x^{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2},
\]
where $\tilde{\varphi}$ is the pullback of $\varphi$ (i.e. its periodic
extension) on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$. It is clear that $F$ has bounded
first and second derivatives on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$. In addition, let
$\eta:=(\cos\alpha_{0},\sin\alpha_{0})^{T}$ and let $\tilde{V}$
be the periodic extension of $V$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ (same for $\tilde{W}_{\alpha_{0}}$).
Then one has 
\[
((\tilde{V}\cdot\eta)F)(x)=\langle dF(x),\tilde{W}_{\alpha_{0}}(x)\rangle=\langle\eta([x]),W_{\alpha_{0}}([x])\rangle\geqslant m>0
\]
for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ ($[x]\in\mathbb{T}^{2}$ denotes the
projected image of $x$). As a consequence, Condition (H) in Section
\ref{sec:LowGauCondYoung} is satisfied with the above choices of
$\eta$ and $F$. The Gaussian lower tail estimate (\ref{eq:GaussLowTorus})
now follows from Theorem {\ref{thm:GLowH}}.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lem-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:HyperSelect}Let $\alpha_{0}\in[0,2\pi)$ be such that
the foliation of $W_{\alpha_{0}}$ contains a Reeb component. Then
there exists $\alpha_{*}\in[0,2\pi)$ such that $W_{\alpha_{*}}$
admits a hyperbolic periodic orbit.
<!-- end lem-24 -->
<!-- lem-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:YoungCty}Let $p\in(1/H,2)$. Consider the differential equation 
\[
\begin{cases}
dY_{s}=\tilde{W}(Y_{s})ds+\tilde{V}(Y_{s})dv_{s}, & 0\leqslant s\leqslant T,\\
Y_{0}=y\in\mathbb{R}^{2},
\end{cases}
\]
where $\tilde{W},\tilde{V}$ are the periodic extension of $W,V\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$
respectively and $v\in C^{p\text{-var}}([0,T];\mathbb{R}^{2})$. For
any $M>0,$ there exists $C>0$ depending only on $V,W,p,T$ and $M,$
such that 
\[
\|v\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M\implies\sup_{0\leqslant s\leqslant T}\big|Y_{s}-\tilde{\phi}_{s}(y)\big|\leqslant C\|v\|_{p\text{-var}}.
\]
Here $\tilde{\phi}_{s}(y)$ denotes the flow of $\tilde{W}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$
starting from $y$.
<!-- end lem-25 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
This is immediate from standard continuity estimates for Young's differential
equations (see e.g. \cite[Theorem 10.38]{FV10}).
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lem-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:OrbitStab}Let $\lambda^{*}\in(\lambda_{\gamma},1)$ be
a given fixed number. Then there exists $\delta<\varepsilon$, such
that 
\begin{equation}
\phi_{s}(U_{\delta})\subseteq U_{\varepsilon/4}\label{eq:Tub1}
\end{equation}
for all $s\in[0,T]$ and 
\begin{equation}
|z(\phi_{T}(x))|\leqslant\lambda^{*}|z(x)|\label{eq:Tub2}
\end{equation}
for all $x\in U_{\delta}$. Here $\phi_{s}$ denotes the flow of $W$.
<!-- end lem-26 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
The property (\ref{eq:Tub1}) is obvious by continuity. To prove the
second property, let 
\[
G(t,r):=z\big(\phi_{T}(\Phi(t,r))\big),\quad(t,r)\times\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}\times(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon).
\]
Note that $\partial_{r}G(t,0)=\lambda_{\gamma}.$ By continuity, one
has 
\[
\sup_{\substack{t\in\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}\\
r\in(-\delta,\delta)
}
}\big|\partial_{r}G(t,r)\big|\leqslant\lambda^{*},
\]
provided that $\delta$ is small enough. Since $G(t,0)=0,$ it follows
that 
\[
|z(\phi_{T}(x))|=\big|G(t,r)\big|\leqslant\int_{0}^{r}\big|\partial_{r}G(t,\rho)\big|d\rho\leqslant\lambda^{*}|r|=\lambda^{*}|z(x)|
\]
for any $x=\Phi(t,r)\in U_{\delta}$. This proves the property (\ref{eq:Tub2}).
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- rem-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:LiftedTube}Due to periodicity, it is clear that both properties
(\ref{eq:Tub1}) and (\ref{eq:Tub2}) remain valid for the lifted
objects on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.
<!-- end rem-10 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
We divide the argument into several major steps. Let $\lambda^{*},U_{\delta}$
be given as in Lemma \ref{lem:OrbitStab}. Let $R>2T$. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) Consider the differential equation 
\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
dX_{t}^{R,w}=R\tilde{W}(X_{t}^{R,w})dt+\tilde{V}(X_{t})dw_{t}, & 1/2\leqslant t\leqslant1,\\
X_{1/2}^{R,w}=x\in\tilde{U}_{\delta},
\end{cases}\label{eq:YoungDE}
\end{equation}
where $w\in C^{p\text{-var}}([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{2})$. We divide $[1/2,1]$
into equal subintervals 
\[
[t_{j-1},t_{j}]:=[1/2+(j-1)T/R,1/2+jT/R],\quad j=1,\cdots,\lfloor\frac{R}{2T}\rfloor:=N_{R}
\]
as well as the last subinterval $[t_{N_{R}},1].$ We claim that there
exists $M_{1}>0$ depending on $\delta,$ such that 
\begin{equation}
\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}\leqslant M_{1}\implies X_{t_{j}}^{R,w}\in\tilde{U}_{\delta}\label{eq:TunStab}
\end{equation}
for all $j=1,\cdots,N_{R}.$

To see this, suppose that $X_{t_{j-1}}^{R,w}\in\tilde{U}_{\delta}$.
One can reparametrise the equation (\ref{eq:YoungDE}) on $[t_{j-1},t_{j}]$
as 
\[
\begin{cases}
dY_{s}^{j}=\tilde{W}(Y_{s}^{j})ds+\tilde{V}(Y_{s}^{j})dv_{s}^{j}, & 0\leqslant s\leqslant T,\\
Y_{0}^{j}=X_{t_{j-1}}^{R,w},
\end{cases}
\]
where $v_{s}^{j}:=w_{t_{j-1}+s/R}-w_{t_{j-1}}.$ Note that 
\[
\|v^{j}\|_{p\text{-var};[0,T]}=\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[t_{j-1},t_{j}]}\leqslant\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}.
\]
By the relation (\ref{eq:Tub1}) (cf. Remark \ref{rem:LiftedTube}),
one has 
\[
\big\{\tilde{\phi}_{s}(X_{t_{j-1}}^{R,w}):0\leqslant s\leqslant T\big\}\subseteq\tilde{U}_{\varepsilon/4}.
\]
In addition, according to Lemma \ref{lem:YoungCty}, one has 
\[
\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}\leqslant1\implies\sup_{0\leqslant s\leqslant T}\big|Y_{s}^{j}-\tilde{\phi}_{s}(X_{t_{j-1}}^{R,w})\big|\leqslant C_{1}\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}.
\]
In particular, $X_{t}^{R,w}\in\tilde{U}_{\varepsilon/2}$ for all
$t\in[t_{j-1},t_{j}]$, provided that $\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}\leqslant M_{1}$
and $M_{1}<\frac{\varepsilon}{4C_{1}}\wedge1.$ 

Note that the transversal coordinate map $z:U_{\varepsilon}\rightarrow(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$
is Lipschitz on $\bar{U}_{\varepsilon/2}$. Let $L$ denote its Lipschitz
constant (same constant for $\tilde{z}$). The previous continuity
estimate also yields that 
\[
\big|\tilde{z}(X_{t_{j}}^{R,w})-\tilde{z}(\tilde{\phi}_{T}(X_{t_{j-1}}^{R,w}))\big|\leqslant C_{1}L\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]},
\]
provided that $\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}\leqslant M_{1}.$ It follows
from the contraction property (\ref{eq:Tub2}) that 
\begin{align*}
\big|\tilde{z}(X_{t_{j}}^{R,w})\big| & \leqslant\big|\tilde{z}(\tilde{\phi}_{T}(X_{t_{j-1}}^{R,w}))\big|+\big|\tilde{z}(X_{t_{j}}^{R,w})-\tilde{z}(\tilde{\phi}_{T}(X_{t_{j-1}}^{R,w}))\big|\\
 & \leqslant\lambda^{*}\delta+C_{1}L\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}\leqslant\lambda^{*}\delta+C_{1}LM_{1}.
\end{align*}
By further requiring 
\[
M_{1}<\frac{(1-\lambda^{*})\delta}{C_{1}L},
\]
one obtains that 
\[
\big|\tilde{z}(X_{t_{j}}^{R,w})\big|<\delta\iff X_{t_{j}}^{R,w}\in\tilde{U}_{\delta}.
\]
Since $X_{1/2}^{R,w}=x\in\tilde{U}_{\delta}$ by assumption, this
proves the claim (\ref{eq:TunStab}) by induction on $j$. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) Since $\gamma$ has nontrivial homology,
there exists $k\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\backslash\{(0,0)\}$ such that 
\[
\tilde{\gamma}(s+T)=\tilde{\gamma}(s)+k
\]
for all $s\in\mathbb{R}.$ Consider the function 
\[
F(x):=\frac{k\cdot x}{|k|^{2}},\quad x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}.
\]
Note that $F(\tilde{\phi}_{T}(x)-x)=1$ for all $x\in\tilde{\gamma}$.
By shrinking $\delta$ if necessary, one can ensure that 
\begin{equation}
F\big(\tilde{\phi}_{T}(x)-x\big)\geqslant\frac{3}{4}\label{eq:LinDispPerOrb}
\end{equation}
for all $x\in\tilde{U}_{\delta}.$

Let $X_{t}^{R,w}$ be the solution to the equation (\ref{eq:YoungDE}).
We claim that there exists $M_{1}>0$, such that 
\begin{equation}
\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}\leqslant M_{1}\implies F\big(X_{t_{j}}^{R,w}-X_{t_{j-1}}^{R}\big)\geqslant\frac{1}{2}\label{eq:LinDispTorus}
\end{equation}
for all $i=1,\cdots,N_{R}.$ Indeed, with $M_{1}$ chosen as in Part
(i) one has 
\[
\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}\leqslant M_{1}\implies\big|F\big(X_{t_{j}}^{R,w}-\tilde{\phi}_{T}(X_{t_{j-1}}^{R,w})\big)\big|\leqslant\frac{C_{1}}{|k|}\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}.
\]
Since $X_{t_{j-1}}^{R,w}\in\tilde{U}_{\delta},$ it follows from (\ref{eq:LinDispPerOrb})
that 
\begin{align*}
F\big(X_{t_{j}}^{R,w}-X_{t_{j-1}}^{R,w}\big) & \geqslant F\big(\tilde{\phi}_{T}(X_{t_{j-1}}^{R,w})-X_{t_{j-1}}^{R,w}\big)-\frac{C_{1}}{|k|}\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}\geqslant\frac{3}{4}-\frac{C_{1}M_{1}}{|k|}.
\end{align*}
By further requiring 
\[
M_{1}<\frac{|k|}{4C_{1}},
\]
one concludes that (\ref{eq:LinDispTorus}) holds. As a consequence,
\[
F\big(X_{t_{N_{R}}}^{R,w}-X_{1/2}^{R,w}\big)\geqslant\frac{1}{2}N_{R}=\frac{1}{2}\lfloor\frac{R}{2T}\rfloor
\]
provided that $X_{1/2}^{R,w}\in\tilde{U}_{\delta}$ and $\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}\leqslant M_{1}.$ 

Under the same assumptions as above, the last piece $[t_{N_{R}},1]$
is easily estimated as 
\begin{align*}
\big|F\big(X_{1}^{R,w}-X_{t_{N_{R}}}^{R,w}\big)\big|\leqslant & C_{2}\sup_{0\leqslant s\leqslant T}\Big[\big|Y_{s}^{N_{R}+1}-\tilde{\phi}_{s}(X_{t_{N_{R}}}^{R,w})\big|\\
 & \ \ \ +\big|\tilde{\phi}_{s}(X_{t_{N_{R}}}^{R,w})-X_{t_{N_{R}}}^{R,w}\big|\Big]\leqslant C_{3}.
\end{align*}
By using the Lipschitz property of $F$ again, one therefore obtains
that 
\begin{equation}
\big|X_{1}^{R,w}-X_{1/2}^{R,w}\big|\geqslant\frac{|k|}{2}\lfloor\frac{R}{2T}\rfloor-C_{3}|k|,\label{eq:LinearTorus}
\end{equation}
provided that $X_{1/2}^{R,w}\in\tilde{U}_{\delta}$ and $\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[1/2,1]}\leqslant M_{1}.$
The estimate (\ref{eq:LinearTorus}) is uniform for all large $R$
(with $M$ being chosen as before). 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iii) Recall that $x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$
is the given initial condition of the SDE (\ref{eq:SDETorus}). Let
$x$ be any fixed point on $\tilde{\gamma}$ and let $\beta:[0,1/2]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$
be any fixed smooth path (e.g. the straight line) such that $\beta_{0}=x_{0},$
$\beta_{1/2}=x$. Define 
\[
h_{\text{int}}(t):=\int_{0}^{t}V^{-1}(\beta_{s})\dot{\beta_{s}ds,\quad}0\leqslant t\leqslant\frac{1}{2}.
\]
By definition, the control $h_{{\rm int}}$ drives the dynamics 
\[
dy_{t}=V(y_{t})\dot{h}_{{\rm int}}(t)dt
\]
from $x_{0}$ to $x$ along $\beta$. By the same continuity estimate
leading to Lemma \ref{lem:YoungCty}, one has 
\[
||w\|_{p\text{-var};[0,1/2]}\leqslant M_{0}\implies X_{1/2}^{w+h_{{\rm int}}}\in\tilde{U}_{\delta}
\]
for some small $M_{0}$. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iv) Let us summarise what we have obtained
so far. For each $R>2T,$ define 
\[
h^{R}(t)\triangleq\hat{h}_{{\rm int}}(t)+R\cdot\hat{h}_{{\rm main}}(t),\quad0\leqslant t\leqslant1,
\]
where 
\[
\hat{h}_{{\rm int}}(t):=\begin{cases}
h_{{\rm int}}(t), & 0\leqslant t\leqslant1/2,\\
h_{{\rm int}}(1/2), & 1/2\leqslant t\leqslant1,
\end{cases}\quad\hat{h}_{{\rm main}}(t):=\begin{cases}
0, & 0\leqslant t\leqslant1/2,\\
(t-1/2)\eta_{*}, & 1/2\leqslant t\leqslant1
\end{cases}
\]
and $\eta_{*}:=(\cos\alpha_{*},\sin\alpha_{*})^{T}.$ Let $M:=M_{0}\wedge M_{1}.$
What we have shown is that whenever $w\in C^{p\text{-var}}([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{2})$
satisfies $\|w\|_{p\text{-var};[0,1]}\leqslant M$, one has 
\[
\big|X_{1}^{w+h^{R}}-x_{0}\big|\geqslant\frac{|k|}{2}\lfloor\frac{R}{2T}\rfloor-C_{3}|k|-|x-x_{0}|
\]
for all large $R$. On the other hand, it is easy to see that $\hat{h}_{{\rm int}},\hat{h}_{{\rm main}}\in\bar{{\cal H}}$
and 
\[
\|h^{R}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}\leqslant\|\hat{h}_{{\rm int}}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}+R\|\hat{h}_{{\rm main}}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}.
\]
These are essentially the properties (\ref{eq:DispEstYoung}) and
(\ref{eq:hRNorm}). Therefore, one can carry through exactly the same
Cameron-Martin transformation argument from the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:GLowH}
to conclude that the solution to the SDE (\ref{eq:SDETorus}) at time
one admits a Gaussian lower tail. 

The proof of Theorem \ref{thm:2DPeriodic} is now complete.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lem-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:NonDegD}One has $\partial_{\alpha}D(0,\alpha_{0})\neq0$.
<!-- end lem-27 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Recall that $\gamma:[0,T]\rightarrow\mathbb{T}^{2}$ ($\gamma_{0}=x$)
is the chosen periodic orbit of $W_{\alpha_{0}}$ from a Reeb component.
Consider the function 
\[
d(t):=\det\big(W_{\alpha_{0}}(\gamma_{t}),\xi(t)\big)
\]
where $\xi(t):=\partial_{\alpha}\phi_{t}^{\alpha}(x)\big|_{\alpha=\alpha_{0}}$.
Let $Z(y):=\partial_{\alpha}W_{\alpha}(y)|_{\alpha=\alpha_{0}}$ for
$y\in\mathbb{T}^{2}.$ By using the flow equation of $\phi_{t}^{\alpha}$,
it is easily seen that 
\[
\dot{\xi}(t)=DW_{\alpha_{0}}(\gamma_{t})\xi(t)+Z(\gamma_{t}),\quad\xi(0)=0.
\]
Therefore, one has 
\begin{align}
\dot{d}(t)= & \det\big((DW_{\alpha_{0}}\cdot W_{\alpha_{0}})(\gamma_{t}),\xi(t)\big)+\det\big(W_{\alpha_{0}}(\gamma_{t}),DW_{\alpha_{0}}(\gamma_{t})\xi(t)\big)\nonumber \\
 & \ \ \ +\det\big(W_{\alpha_{0}}(\gamma_{t}),Z(\gamma_{t})\big)\nonumber \\
= & \big({\rm div}W_{\alpha_{0}}\big)(\gamma_{t})\cdot d(t)+\det\big(W_{\alpha_{0}}(\gamma_{t}),Z(\gamma_{t})\big).\label{eq:dtODE}
\end{align}
To reach the last equality, we used the simple relation that 
\[
\det(A\cdot{\bf u},{\bf v})+\det({\bf u},A\cdot{\bf v})={\rm tr}[A]\det({\bf u},{\bf v})
\]
for any $2\times2$ matrix $A$ and $2\times1$ row vectors ${\bf u},{\bf v}$.
Since $d(0)=0,$ it follows from (\ref{eq:dtODE}) that 
\[
d(T)=\int_{0}^{T}\exp\Big[\int_{s}^{T}({\rm div}W_{\alpha_{0}})(\gamma(r))dr\Big]\det\big(W_{\alpha_{0}}(\gamma_{s}),Z(\gamma_{s})\big)ds.
\]
Explicit computation shows that 
\[
\det\big(W_{\alpha_{0}}(y),Z(y)\big)=\det V(y)
\]
for all $y\in\mathbb{T}^{2}$. Since $V$ is uniformly elliptic, the above determinant has a constant sign. As a 
consequence, $d(T)\neq 0$.

On the other hand, by differentiating the relation (\ref{eq:ParaPoinMap})
with respect to $\alpha$ at $(u,\alpha)=(0,\alpha_{0})$, one finds
that 
\[
\xi(T)+\partial_{\alpha}\tau(0,\alpha_{0})W_{\alpha_{0}}(x)=\partial_{\alpha}P(0,\alpha_{0})\cdot\sigma'(0).
\]
By taking determinant with $W_{\alpha_{0}}(\gamma_{T})=W_{\alpha_{0}}(x),$
it follows that
\[
d(T)=\partial_{\alpha}P(0,\alpha_{0})\cdot\det\big(W_{\alpha_{0}}(x),\sigma'(0)\big).
\]
Since $\Sigma$ intersects $\gamma$ transversally at $x$, one knows
that 
\[
\det\big(W_{\alpha_{0}}(x),\sigma'(0)\big)\neq0.
\]
Therefore, 
\[
\partial_{\alpha}D(0,\alpha_{0})=\partial_{\alpha}P(0,\alpha_{0})\neq0.
\]
This completes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lem-28: body_md -->
There exists a $u_{*}\in(0,\delta_{1})$, such that the orbit of $W_{A(u_{*})}$
passing through $\sigma(u_*)$ is hyperbolic.
<!-- end lem-28 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
By differentiating (\ref{eq:IFT}), one finds that 
\[
\partial_{u}D(u,A(u))+\partial_{\alpha}D(u,A(u))A'(u)=0
\]
for all $u\in(-\delta_{1},\delta_{1})$. For $u\in(0,\delta_{1})$,
recall that the orbit of $W_{\alpha_{0}}$ through $\sigma(u)$ is
nonperiodic by assumption (because it is a leaf inside the interior of the Reeb component
$A$). In particular, one has $D(u,\alpha_{0})\neq0$ and
therefore, $A(u)\neq\alpha_{0}$ for any $u\in(0,\delta_{1})$. Since
$A(0)=\alpha_{0}$, it follows that for any $\eta>0,$ there exists
$u_{\eta}\in(0,\eta)$ such that $A'(u_{\eta})\neq0$. On the other
hand, one knows from Lemma \ref{lem:NonDegD} and continuity that
$\partial_{\alpha}D(u,A(u))\neq0$ for all sufficiently small $u$.
As a consequence, there must exist $u_{*}\in(0,\delta_{1})$, such
that 
\[
\partial_{u}D(u_{*},A(u_{*}))\neq0,
\]
or equivalently, $\partial_{u}P(u_{*},\alpha_{*})\neq1$ where $\alpha_{*}:=A(u_{*})$.
By definition, one concludes that the periodic orbit of $W_{\alpha_{*}}$
through $\sigma(u_{*})$ is hyperbolic.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- rem-11: body_md -->
Although the suspension case is relatively simple, one cannot expect
avoiding the Reeb component case by hoping that ``there always exists
$\alpha\in[0,2\pi)$ such that $W_{\alpha}$ does not contain a Reeb
component''. For instance, consider the elliptic system
\[
V(x)=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\cos2\pi x^{1} & -\sin2\pi x^{1}\\
\sin2\pi x^{1} & \cos2\pi x^{1}
\end{array}\right),\quad x=(x^{1},x^{2})\in\mathbb{T}^{2}.
\]
One has 
\[
W_{\alpha}(x)=\left(\begin{array}{c}
\cos(2\pi x^{1}+\alpha)\\
\sin(2\pi x^{1}+\alpha)
\end{array}\right)
\]for every $\alpha\in[0,2\pi)$. 
In particular, the foliation of $W_{\alpha}$ contains precisely two
Reeb components bounded by the compact leaves (periodic orbits) 
\[
L_{+}:x^{1}=\frac{\pi/2-\alpha}{2\pi},\quad L_{-}:x^{1}=\frac{3\pi/2-\alpha}{2\pi}
\]
respectively, regardless of the value of $\alpha$.
<!-- end rem-11 -->
<!-- rem-12: body_md -->
Both Theorem \ref{thm:2DCounter} and Theorem \ref{thm:2DPeriodic} are concerned with periodic systems. The essential reason behind their qualitatively different tail behaviours can be summarised as follows. 

For the radially periodic example, when the system propagates through annuli, one encounters new geometry and there is no simple ballistic tunnel that the system could use. Any large distance propagation has to cause sufficiently many effective turns for the control.

On the other hand, for the torus system, there is always either a globally monotone direction (suspension case) or a periodic orbit on the fundamental domain $\mathbb{T}^2$ with nontrivial homology,  which can be reused by the system precisely due to the repeating geometry  the system encounters when it propagates through different fundamental domains. Both cases lead to a global ballistic tunnel with a small growth of Cameron-Martin norm.
<!-- end rem-12 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:VFFolia}The family ${\cal F}_{W}$ defines a 1D foliation
on $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ in the sense of Definition \ref{def:Folia}.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
It is clear that ${\cal F}_{W}$ is a family of immersed 1D manifolds
whose union is $\mathbb{T}^{2}.$ To prove the local flatness property,
let $x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}.$ Since $W(x)\neq0,$ one can pick a nonzero
vector $v\in T_{x}\mathbb{T}^{2}$ that is linearly independent of
$W(x).$ Let $\sigma:(-\delta,\delta)\rightarrow\mathbb{T}^{2}$ be
a smooth arc such that $\sigma(0)=x,$ $\dot{\sigma}(0)=v$. Define
\[
F:\mathbb{R}\times(-\delta,\delta)\rightarrow\mathbb{T}^{2},\quad F(t,r):=\phi_{t}(\sigma(r)).
\]
It is clear that $F(0,0)=x$ and $(dF)_{(0,0)}$ is nonsingular. Therefore,
$F$ is a local diffeomorphism from $V:=(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\times(-\delta',\delta')$
onto $F(V)$ with some small $\varepsilon$ and $\delta'<\delta$.
The map $F|_{V}$ provides a flat chart of $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ around
$x$; each horizontal arc $s\mapsto(s,r)$ corresponds to a flow line
by definition and every flow line inside $F(V)$ must come from a
horizontal arc since $W=\partial_{s}$ in $F(V)$.\textcolor{blue}{{} }
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- rem-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:FlowVSFolia}The actual flow $\{\phi_{t}(x)\}$ carries
more information than the foliation ${\cal F}_{W}$ itself; the foliation
is determined by the \textit{1D distribution} $\{{\rm Span}W(x):x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}\}$
while the flow also records the orientation and the strength of the
field.
<!-- end rem-13 -->
<!-- defn-12: body_md -->
The leaf ${\cal O}_{x}:=\{\phi_{t}(x):t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ is called
the \textit{orbit} of $W$ passing through $x$. An orbit ${\cal O}_{x}$
is said to be \textit{periodic} if it is a compact leaf.
<!-- end defn-12 -->
<!-- defn-13: body_md -->
Let $P,Q$ be two oriented, embedded 1D submanifolds of $\mathbb{T}^{2}.$
We say that $P$ is \textit{transversal} to $Q$ if $T_{x}P$ and
$T_{x}Q$ (as 1D subspaces of $T_{x}\mathbb{T}^{2}$) are linearly
independent at every $x\in P\cap Q$. In this case, the \textit{local
intersection number} of $P$ and $Q$ at $x\in P\cap Q$ is defined
by 
\[
i_{x}(P,Q):=\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if }\det(v_{x},w_{x})>0;\\
-1, & \text{if }\det(v_{x},w_{x})<0,
\end{cases}
\]
where $v_{x}$ (respectively, $w_{x}$) is any positively oriented
vector in $T_{x}P$ (respectively, $T_{x}Q$). The \textit{intersection
number} of $P$ and $Q$ is defined by 
\[
I(P,Q):=\sum_{x\in P\cap Q}i_{x}(P,Q),
\]
provided further that $P\cap Q$ is a finite set.
<!-- end defn-13 -->
<!-- lem-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:IntNumForm}Let $P,Q$ be smooth, simple and closed curves
which intersect transversally and whose homology classes are given
by 
\begin{equation}
[P]=p_{1}\sigma_{1}+p_{2}\sigma_{2},\quad[Q]=q_{1}\sigma_{1}+q_{2}\sigma_{2},\label{eq:IntNumAssump}
\end{equation}
with $p_{i},q_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then $I(P,Q)=p_{1}q_{2}-p_{2}q_{1}$.
<!-- end lem-29 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Let 
\[
P=\left(\begin{array}{c}
P_{1}\\
P_{2}
\end{array}\right),Q=\left(\begin{array}{c}
Q_{1}\\
Q_{2}
\end{array}\right):S^{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{T}^{2}
\]
be parametrised by $S^{1}:=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}.$ Consider the map
$D:S^{1}\times S^{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{T}^{2}$ defined by 
\[
D(s,t):=P(s)-Q(t)\quad({\rm mod\ \mathbb{Z}}).
\]
At each intersection point $(s,t)\in D^{-1}(0),$ by the transversal
intersection assumption one has 
\[
\det\big((dD)_{(s,t)}\big)=-\det\big(\dot{P}(s),\dot{Q}(t)\big)\neq0.
\]
Therefore, $0$ is a regular value of $D$. It follows that $D^{-1}(0)$
is a zero-dimensional submanifold of $S^{1}\times S^{1}$. Hence,
it is a finite set of points, say 
\[
D^{-1}(0)=\{(s_{1},t_{1}),\cdots,(s_{k},t_{k})\}.
\]
There exists a neighbourhood $U_{k}$ of $(s_{k},t_{k})$ for each
$k$ and a neighbourhood $V$ of $0$, such that $D|_{U_{k}}$ is
a diffeomorphism from $U_{k}$ onto $V$. In addition, one has 
\[
{\rm sgn}\det\big((dD)_{(s_{k},t_{k})}\big)=-{\rm sgn}\det\big(\dot{P}(s_{k}),\dot{Q}(t_{k})\big)=-i_{x_{k}}(P,Q),
\]
where $x_{k}:=P(s_{k})=Q(t_{k})$. 

Let $\omega$ be a smooth $2$-form that is compactly supported inside
$V$ and satisfies $\int_{V}\omega=1$. Since $D|_{U_{k}}:U_{k}\rightarrow V$
is a diffeomorphism, one has 
\[
\int_{U_{k}}D|_{U_{k}}^{*}\omega={\rm sgn}\det\big((dD)_{(s_{k},t_{k})}\big)\int_{V}\omega=-i_{x_{k}}(P,Q).
\]
Therefore, 
\[
\int_{S^{1}\times S^{1}}D^{*}\omega=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\int_{U_{k}}D|_{U_{k}}^{*}\omega=-I(P,Q).
\]
Let $\nu=dx\wedge dy\in\Omega^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$. Since both $\omega$
and $\nu$ are closed and have the same integral on $\mathbb{T}^{2}$
(which is equal to one), they differ by an exact form. As a result,
\begin{equation}
\int_{S^{1}\times S^{1}}D^{*}\nu=\int_{S^{1}\times S^{1}}D^{*}\omega=-I(P,Q).\label{eq:IntNumPf1}
\end{equation}
Now it remains to compute the integral of $D^{*}\nu$.

By using the explicit expressions of $D$ and $\nu,$ it is plain
to check that 
\[
D^{*}\nu=\big(P_{2}'(s)Q_{1}'(t)-P_{1}'(s)Q_{2}'(t)\big)ds\wedge dt.
\]
Therefore, 
\begin{align*}
\int_{S^{1}\times S^{1}}D^{*}\nu & =\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\big(P_{2}'(s)Q_{1}'(t)-P_{1}'(s)Q_{2}'(t)\big)dsdt\\
 & =\Big(\int_{0}^{1}P_{2}'(s)ds\Big)\Big(\int_{0}^{1}Q_{1}'(t)dt\Big)-\Big(\int_{0}^{1}P_{1}'(s)ds\Big)\Big(\int_{0}^{1}Q_{2}'(t)dt\Big).
\end{align*}
Let $\tilde{P},\tilde{Q}$ be some lifts of $P,Q$ on the universal
cover $\mathbb{R}^{2}$. According to the assumption (\ref{eq:IntNumAssump}),
one has
\[
\int_{0}^{1}P'(s)ds=\int_{0}^{1}\tilde{P}'(s)ds=\tilde{P}(1)-\tilde{P}(0)=(p_{1},p_{2}),
\]
\[
\int_{0}^{1}Q'(t)dt=\int_{0}^{1}\tilde{Q}'(t)dt=\tilde{Q}(1)-\tilde{Q}(0)=(q_{1},q_{2}).
\]
As a consequence, 
\begin{equation}
\int_{S^{1}\times S^{1}}D^{*}\nu=p_{2}q_{1}-p_{1}q_{2}.\label{eq:IntNumPf2}
\end{equation}
The conclusion of the lemma follows from the relations (\ref{eq:IntNumPf1})
and (\ref{eq:IntNumPf2}).
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- rem-14: body_md -->
\label{rem:IntNumNoInt}Lemma \ref{lem:IntNumForm} remains valid
if $P\cap Q=\emptyset.$ In this case, $I(P,Q)=p_{1}q_{2}-p_{2}q_{1}=0$.
<!-- end rem-14 -->
<!-- defn-14: body_md -->
A (continuous) closed curve $\gamma$ in $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ is said
to be \textit{essential} if its (singular) homology class $[\gamma]\in H_{1}(\mathbb{T}^{2};\mathbb{Z})$
is nonzero. It is \textit{primitive} if its homology class cannot
be expressed as $[\gamma]=m\sigma$ for some $\sigma\in H_{1}(\mathbb{T}^{2};\mathbb{Z})$
and $m\geqslant2.$
<!-- end defn-14 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:POTop}(i) Every periodic orbit is essential.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) Every essential, simple closed curve is
primitive. In particular, every periodic orbit is primitive. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iii) For any pair of periodic orbits $\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},$
one has $[\gamma_{1}]=\pm[\gamma_{2}]$.
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
(i) Let $\gamma$ be a periodic orbit of $W$. Suppose on the contrary
that $[\gamma]=0.$ Since $\gamma$ is simple closed, it must bound
a topological disk $D$ in this case. According to the Poincar\'e-Hopf
theorem for the disk $D$ (see \cite[Chapter 3, Theorem 2]{Per13}),
one has 
\[
{\rm ind}_{W}(\partial D)=\sum_{z\in{\cal Z}(W)\cap \mathrm{int}D}{\rm ind}_{W}(z).
\]
Here ${\rm ind}_{W}(\partial D)$ denotes the index of $W$ on the
boundary $\partial D$ and ${\rm ind}_{W}(z)$ denotes the local index
of $W$ at the zero $z$ (${\cal Z}(W)$ denotes the set of zeros
of $W$). It is plain from the definition that ${\rm ind}_{W}(\partial D)=\pm1$
(the sign depends on the orientation convention of $\gamma$). As
a result, $W$ must have at least one zero in the interior of $D$.
This is a contradiction. Therefore, $[\gamma]\neq0$.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) Let $\gamma$ be an essential, simple
closed curve. We claim that $\mathbb{T}^{2}\backslash\gamma$ is connected.
Suppose on the contrary that $\mathbb{T}^{2}\backslash\gamma$ is
disconnected. Let $N\cong S^{1}\times(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$
be a tubular neighbourhood of $\gamma$. Then 
\[
N_{-}:=S^{1}\times(-\varepsilon,0),\quad N_{+}:=S^{1}\times(0,\varepsilon)
\]
must be contained in different components of $\mathbb{T}^{2}\backslash\gamma$;
otherwise, any other component $V$ would intersect this component
(because $\gamma\subseteq\bar{V}$) which contradicts disconnectedness.
Let $U_{+}$ be the component containing $N_{+}.$ Since $N_{-}$
is contained in a different component, $\overline{U_{+}}$ is a compact
surface with boundary $\gamma$. As a consequence, $\gamma=\partial c$
for some singular $2$-chain. It follows that $[\gamma]=0$ which
leads to a contradiction. Therefore, $\mathbb{T}^{2}\backslash\gamma$
is connected.

Pick two points $x_{+}\in N_{+}$ and $x_{-}\in N_{-}.$ Draw a smooth,
simple curve $\eta$ from $x_{+}$ to $x_{-}$ inside $\mathbb{T}^{2}\backslash\gamma$
(which is possible due to connectedness). Let $\sigma$ be a simple
arc which joins $x_{+}$ to $x_{-}$ inside $N$. By smoothing the
corners and removing loops from $\eta\sqcup\sigma$ if necessary,
one obtains a simple closed curve $\beta$ that has precisely one
(transversal) intersection with $\gamma$. Therefore, 
\begin{equation}
I(\gamma,\beta)=\pm1.\label{eq:PrimPf}
\end{equation}
Suppose that $\gamma$ is not primitive. Under the canonical basis
$\{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\}$ of $H_{1}(\mathbb{T}^{2};\mathbb{Z})$,
one can write $[\gamma]=m(p,q)$ for some $m\geqslant2$ and $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}$.
Let $[\beta]=(r,s)$. According to Lemma \ref{lem:IntNumForm}, one
has 
\[
I(\gamma,\beta)=m(ps-qr).
\]
This contradicts the fact that (\ref{eq:PrimPf}). Therefore, $\gamma$
is primitive. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iii) Let $\gamma_{1}=(p,q)$ and $\gamma_{2}=(r,s)$
be two periodic orbits. Since $\gamma_{1}$ is primitive by Part (ii),
the integers $p,q$ are coprime. Similarly, $r,s$ is also coprime.
Since $\gamma_{1}\cap\gamma_{2}=\emptyset$, one knows from Lemma
\ref{lem:IntNumForm} (cf. Remark \ref{rem:IntNumNoInt}) that 
\[
(p,q)=\frac{a}{b}(r,s)
\]
for some coprime pair $(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$. In particular, 
\[
ar=bp,\quad as=bq.
\]
It follows that $a|p$ and $a|q$ which implies that $a=\pm1$. Similarly,
$b=\pm1$. Therefore, $[\gamma_{1}]=\pm[\gamma_{2}]$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lem-30: body_md -->
\label{lem:PoinMap}There exists a small neighbourhood $U\subseteq\Sigma$
of $x$, such that $(\tau(y),P(y))$ is well-defined for all $y\in U$.
In addition, both $\tau(y)$, $P(y)$ are smooth on $U$ and one has
$\tau(x)=T,$ $P(x)=x.$
<!-- end lem-30 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
First of all, there exists a neighbourhood $U_{0}\subseteq\Sigma$
of $x$, such that $U_{0}$ is represented by the level set $\{\rho=0\}$
of some smooth function $\rho$ near $x$. Now consider the function
\[
F:U_{0}\times(T-\delta_{0},T+\delta_{0})\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\quad F(y,t):=\rho(\phi_{t}(y))
\]
where $\delta_{0}$ is small. Note that $F(x,T)=0.$ In addition,
since $T_{x}\Sigma=\ker(d\rho)_{x}$ and $\Sigma$ intersects $\gamma$
transversally at $x$, one has 
\begin{equation}
\partial_{t}F(x,T)=\big\langle(d\rho)_{x},W(x)\big\rangle\neq0.\label{eq:PMPf}
\end{equation}
According to the implicit function theorem, there exists $U_{1}\subseteq U_{0}$,
$\delta_{1}<\delta_{0}$ and a smooth function $\tau:U_{1}\rightarrow(T-\delta_{1},T+\delta_{1})$
such that $\tau(x)=T$ and 
\[
F(y,\tau(y))=0
\]
for all $y\in U_{1}$. 

We claim that by shrinking $U_{1}$ to some smaller neighbourhood
$U$ of $x$ if necessary, one has 
\[
\tau(y)=\inf\{t>0:\phi_{t}(y)\in\Sigma\}
\]
for all $y\in U.$ First of all, according to (\ref{eq:PMPf}) there
exists $U_{2}\subseteq U_{1}$ and $\delta_{2}<\delta_{1},$ such
that $t\mapsto F(y,t)$ is strictly monotone on $[T-\delta_{2},T+\delta_{2}]$
for all $y\in U_{2}.$ As a result, $\tau(y)$ is the unique $t\in[T-\delta_{2},T+\delta_{2}]$
such that $F(y,t)=0$. We fix this $\delta_{2}$ in what follows.
Next, by using a flow box argument, there exists $U_{3}\subseteq U_{2}$
and $\varepsilon>0,$ such that $\phi_{t}(y)\notin\Sigma$ for all
$y\in U_{3}$ and $t\in(0,\varepsilon]$. In addition, since 
\[
\big\{\phi_{t}(x):\varepsilon\leqslant t\leqslant T-\delta_{2}\big\}\cap\Sigma=\emptyset,
\]
one knows from continuity that $\phi_{t}(y)\notin\Sigma$ for all
$y$ in some smaller $U\subseteq U_{3}$ and all $t\in[\varepsilon,T-\delta_{2}]$.
Combining the above three scenarios, it follows that $\tau(y)$ is
the first return time of $\phi_{t}(y)$ to $\Sigma$ for every $y\in U$. 

Consequently, the map 
\[
P:U\rightarrow\Sigma,\quad P(y):=\phi_{\tau(y)}(y)
\]
is well-defined. Its smoothness follows immediately from the smoothness
of $\tau$ and the joint smoothness of $(t,y)\mapsto\phi_{t}(y)$.
This completes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- defn-15: body_md -->
The map $P$ constructed above is known as the \textit{Poincar\'e
map} at $x\in\gamma$ with respect to the transversal $\Sigma$.
<!-- end defn-15 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:CharaNum}The number $\lambda_{\gamma}$ does not depend
on the point $x\in\gamma$ or the transversal $\Sigma.$ In addition,
one has $\lambda_{\gamma}>0$.
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
We give an alternative intrinsic construction of $\lambda_{\gamma}$. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) Define the function $J_{t}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$
by 
\[
\phi_{t}^{*}\mu_{g}=J_{t}\mu_{g},
\]
where $\mu_{g}$ denotes the Riemannian volume form on the (oriented)
annulus $\mathbb{T}^{2}$. It is not hard to see that $J_{t}(x)=\det(d\phi_{t})_{x}$,
where the determinant is defined with respect to any positively oriented
orthonormal bases of $T_{x}\mathbb{T}^{2}$ and $T_{\phi_{t}(x)}\mathbb{T}^{2}$.
We claim that 
\begin{equation}
J_{t}(x)=\exp\Big[\int_{0}^{t}({\rm div}_{g}W)(\phi_{s}(x))ds\Big],\quad\text{(Liouville's formula)}\label{eq:Jtx}
\end{equation}
where ${\rm div}_{g}$ denotes the Riemannian divergence. To this
end, one first recalls the following standard Riemannian geometry
fact: 
\[
{\cal L}_{W}\mu_{g}=({\rm div}_{g}W)\mu_{g}.
\]
In addition, by the definition of the Lie derivative, one has 
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\big(\phi_{t}^{*}\mu_{g}\big)=\phi_{t}^{*}\big({\cal L}_{W}\mu_{g}\big).
\]
As a consequence, 
\begin{equation}
\dot{J}_{t}(x)=\big({\rm div}_{g}W\big)(\phi_{t}(x))J_{t}(x).\label{eq:JODE}
\end{equation}
Since $J_{0}(x)=1$, the desired relation (\ref{eq:Jtx}) follows
by solving the ODE (\ref{eq:JODE}). 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) Suppose that $\gamma$ is a periodic orbit
of $W$ with period $T.$ According to Part (i), one has 
\begin{equation}
\det(d\phi_{T})_{x}=\exp\Big[\int_{0}^{T}({\rm div}_{g}W)(\phi_{s}(x))ds\Big].\label{eq:Detdphi}
\end{equation}
In particular, $\det(d\phi_{T})_{x}$ is independent of $x$. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iii) Under the assumption of Part (ii), let
$\Sigma$ be a transversal curve through $x\in\gamma.$ Let $v\in T_{x}\Sigma$
be a nonzero vector. By the definition of the Poincar\'e map, one
has 
\[
P(y)=\phi_{\tau(y)}(y),\quad y\in U\subseteq\Sigma.
\]
It follows from the definition of $\lambda_{\gamma}$ that 
\[
\lambda_{\gamma}v=(dP)_{x}v=(d\phi_{T})_{x}v+\langle d\tau,v\rangle_{x}W(x).
\]
Also note that $(d\phi_{T})_{x}W(x)=W(x)$ since $\gamma$ is a periodic
orbit. Therefore, the matrix of $(d\phi_{T})_{x}:T_{x}\mathbb{T}^{2}\rightarrow T_{x}\mathbb{T}^{2}$
with respect to the basis $\{W(x),v\}$ is given by 
\[
(d\phi_{T})_{x}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
1 & -\langle d\tau,v\rangle_{x}\\
0 & \lambda_{\gamma}
\end{array}\right).
\]
This shows that $\det(d\phi_{T})_{x}=\lambda_{\gamma}.$ In particular,
$\lambda_{\gamma}$ is independent of $x$ and $\Sigma$. The positivity
of $\lambda_{\gamma}$ follows directly from the relation (\ref{eq:Detdphi}).
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- defn-16: body_md -->
The number $\lambda_{\gamma}$ is called the \textit{transverse characteristic
number} of $\gamma.$ A periodic orbit $\gamma$ is said to be hyperbolic
if $\lambda_{\gamma}\neq1$.
<!-- end defn-16 -->
<!-- rem-15: body_md -->
Hyperbolic periodic orbits have strong dynamical stability (exponential
attraction of nearby orbits in the case $\lambda_{\gamma}\in(0,1)$).
Such a stability property is used in the paper \cite{BGW26} to establish
a Gaussian lower tail estimate for 2D periodic, uniformly elliptic
systems driven by a fractional Brownian motion.
<!-- end rem-15 -->
<!-- defn-17: body_md -->
Let $x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}$. The \textit{forward orbit} passing through
$x$ is defined by 
\[
{\cal O}_{x}^{+}:=\{\phi_{t}(x):t\geqslant0\}.
\]
The \textit{forward limit set} of $x$ is defined by 
\[
\omega(x):=\bigcap_{T>0}\overline{\{\phi_{t}(x):t\geqslant T\}}.
\]
One can define the \textit{backward orbit} ${\cal O}_{x}^{-}$ and
the \textit{backward limit set} $\alpha(x)$ in a similar way. A set
$\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{T}^{2}$ is \textit{$W$-invariant} if $\phi_{t}\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda$
for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$.
<!-- end defn-17 -->
<!-- thm-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:PB} Let $X$
be a smooth,  nonvanishing vector field on a planar domain $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2}.$
Let $x\in U$ be given fixed. Suppose that the flow $\phi_{t}(x)$
of $X$ exists for all $t\geqslant0$ and 
\[
\{\phi_{t}(x):t\geqslant0\}\subseteq K
\]
for some compact set $K\Subset U$. Then there exists a periodic orbit
$C\subseteq K$ such that $\omega(x)=C$. A similar assertion holds
for $\alpha(x)$.
<!-- end thm-11 -->
<!-- rem-16: body_md -->
The planar assumption is crucial here; it is certainly possible for
a vector field on $U=\mathbb{T}^{2}$ to have no periodic orbits.
<!-- end rem-16 -->
<!-- lem-31: body_md -->
\label{lem:MonoLem}Let $X$ be a smooth, nonvanishing vector field
on a planar domain $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2}$. Let $\gamma$ be a
nonperiodic orbit of $X$ which exists in $U$ for all $t$. Suppose
that 
\[
V=\big\{(s,r):-\delta_{1}<s<\delta_{2},-\delta_{2}<r<\delta_{2}\big\}
\]
is a local flow box, so that $X=\partial_{s}$ in $V$ and 
\[
\Sigma:=\big\{(s,r):s=0,-\delta_{2}<r<\delta_{2}\big\}
\]
is the vertical transversal. Let $0\leqslant t_{1}<t_{2}<\cdots$
be a sequence of times such that $z_{j}:=\gamma_{t_{j}}\in\Sigma$
and $\gamma_{t}\notin\Sigma$ for all $t\in(t_{j-1},t_{j})$. Then
either 
\[
z_{1}<z_{2}<z_{3}<\cdots
\]
or 
\[
z_{1}>z_{2}>z_{3}>\cdots.
\]
Here we identify $\Sigma$ with its parametrisation interval $(-\delta_{2},\delta_{2})$.
<!-- end lem-31 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Let $z_{0}<z_{1}$. Suppose on the contrary that $z_{2}<z_{1}$. There
are two cases to discuss.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent \textit{\uline{Case I: \mbox{$z_{2}\in(z_{0},z_{1}).$}}} 

\vspace{2mm} Let $\Gamma_{01}$ be the concatenation of $\gamma_{(t_{0},t_{1})}\subseteq\Sigma^{c}$
and the arc connecting $z_{1}$ to $z_{0}$ along $\Sigma$. Then
$\Gamma_{01}$ is a simple closed curve. According to the Jordan curve
theorem, $\Gamma_{0,1}$ divides the plane into a bounded domain $D_{1}$
and an unbounded domain $D_{2}$. Since $\gamma_{t_{1}+\varepsilon}\in D_{2}$
for small $\varepsilon$, one knows by connectedness that $\gamma|_{(t_{1},t_{2})}\subseteq D_{2}$.
However, since $z_{2}\in(z_{0},z_{1})$, one must have $\gamma_{t_{2}-\varepsilon}\in D_{1}$
due to the flow line pattern inside the flow box $V$. This is a contraction. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent \textit{\uline{Case II: \mbox{$z_{2}<z_{0}$}.}} 

\vspace{2mm} Let $\Gamma_{12}$ be the concatenation of $\gamma_{(t_{1},t_{2})}\subseteq\Sigma^{c}$
and the arc connecting $z_{2}$ to $z_{1}$ along $\Sigma$. Then
$\Gamma_{12}$ divides the plane into a bounded domain $D_{1}$ and
an unbounded one $D_{2}.$ Note that $\gamma_{t_{1}-\varepsilon}\in D_{1}$
for small $\varepsilon$ and thus $\gamma_{(t_{0},t_{1})}\subseteq D_{1}.$
This is a contradiction since $\gamma_{t_{0}+\varepsilon}\in D_{2}$
for small $\varepsilon$. \begin{figure}[H] 
\begin{center}  
\includegraphics[scale=0.16]{jordan} 
\end{center}
\end{figure}\noindent Therefore, one concludes that $z_{2}>z_{1}$. The case
when $z_{0}>z_{1}$ is treated in a similar way.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- lem-32: body_md -->
\label{lem:PRPerOrb}Let $X$ be a smooth,  nonvanishing vector field
on a planar domain $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2}$. Let $y\in U$ be a
positively recurrent point of $X$ and assume that $\phi_{t}(y)$
exists in $U$ for all time. Then ${\cal O}_{y}$ is a periodic orbit.
<!-- end lem-32 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Suppose on the contrary that ${\cal O}_{y}$ is a nonperiodic orbit.
Let $V$ be a flow box centered at $y$. Since $y\in\omega(y),$ there
exists a sequence $t_{n}\rightarrow\infty$ such that $\phi_{t_{n}}(y)\rightarrow y$.
Inside the flow box $V$, one may adjust the time $t_{n}$ to some
$s_{n}$ (for all large $n$, say $n>N$) so that 
\[
s_{n}\rightarrow\infty,\quad\phi_{s_{n}}(y)\in\Sigma\text{ are all distinct},\quad\phi_{s_{n}}(y)\rightarrow y.
\]
Note that it takes a uniformly positive amount of time for the flow
line to leave the flow box once it is on $\Sigma$. As a result, there
are at most finitely many return times to $\Sigma$ between $0$ and
$s_{N+1}$. It follows from Lemma \ref{lem:MonoLem} that the sequence
\[
y=\phi_{0}(y),\phi_{s_{N+1}}(y),\phi_{s_{N+2}}(y),\cdots
\]
is monotone on $\Sigma$. This contradicts the fact that $\phi_{s_{n}}(y)\rightarrow y$
as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Therefore, ${\cal O}_{y}$ is a periodic
orbit.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- lem-33: body_md -->
\label{lem:OmeLimPerOrb}Let $X$ be a smooth nonvanishing vector
field on a planar domain $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2}.$ Let $x\in U$
be given fixed. Suppose that the flow $\phi_{t}(x)$ of $X$ exists
for all $t\geqslant0$. Let $C$ be a periodic orbit such that $C\cap\omega(x)\neq\emptyset$.
Then $\omega(x)=C.$
<!-- end lem-33 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
If ${\cal O}_{x}$ is periodic, one trivially has $\omega(x)={\cal O}_{x}=C$.
We therefore assume that ${\cal O}_{x}$ is nonperiodic. By assumption,
let $p\in C\cap\omega(x)$. Then $\phi_{t_{n}}(x)\rightarrow p$ for
some $t_{n}\rightarrow\infty.$ We first claim that $C\subseteq\omega(x)$.
Let $q\in C$. One can write $q=\phi_{t}(p)$ for some $t\geqslant0.$
It follows that $\phi_{t_{n}+t}(x)\rightarrow q$, which implies that
$q\in\omega(x)$. Therefore, $C\subseteq\omega(x)$. 

Conversely, let $q\notin C.$ Our aim is to show that $q\notin\omega(x)$.
Since $C$ is compact, it suffices to show that 
\begin{equation}
\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}d(\phi_{t}(x),C)=0.\label{eq:OrbAsymC}
\end{equation}
To this end, let $V$ be a flow box centered at $p$ with transversal
$\Sigma$. Since $\phi_{t_{n}}(x)\rightarrow p$ and ${\cal O}_{x}$
is nonperiodic, similar to the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:PRPerOrb},
one can find a sequence $s_{n}\rightarrow\infty$ such that the following
properties hold true:

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) $z_{n}:=\phi_{s_{n}}(x)\in\Sigma$ and
$\phi_{s_{n}}(x)\rightarrow p$;

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) $\phi_{t}(x)\notin\Sigma$ for $t\in(s_{n-1},s_{n})$;

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iii) the sequence $z_{1},z_{2},z_{3},\cdots$
is monotone on $\Sigma.$\begin{figure}[H] 
\begin{center}  
\includegraphics[scale=0.14]{lim_po} 
\end{center}
\end{figure}\noindent Consequently, one has 
\begin{equation}
z_{n}\downarrow p\quad\text{or}\quad z_{n}\uparrow p\quad\text{on }\Sigma.\label{eq:MonoPerObLemPf}
\end{equation}
Note that $z_{n+1}=P(z_{n})$ for all sufficiently large $n,$ where
$P$ is the Poincar\'e map defined in Section \ref{subsec:PoinMap}.
By the continuity of the Poincar\'e map, one has 
\begin{equation}
\lim_{z\rightarrow p}\sup_{0\leqslant t\leqslant\tau(z)}d(\phi_{t}(z),C)=0,\label{eq:1IterAsymp}
\end{equation}
where $\tau(z)$ is the first return time of $\phi_{t}(z)$ to $\Sigma$.
The claim (\ref{eq:OrbAsymC}) is now a simple consequence of the
monotone convergence property (\ref{eq:MonoPerObLemPf}) and the one-iteration
asymptotics (\ref{eq:1IterAsymp}).
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- rem-17: body_md -->
Lemma \ref{lem:OmeLimPerOrb} remains valid on the torus $\mathbb{T}^{2}.$
In fact, by cutting $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ along the periodic orbit $C,$
one obtains an annulus $A\cong S^{1}\times[0,1]$ whose two boundary
curves are copies of $C$ and ${\cal O}_{x}\subseteq{\rm int}A$ (assuming
${\cal O}_{x}$ is nonperiodic). By thickening $A$ across its boundary
to an open annulus $U$ ($U$ is diffeomorphic to a planar domain),
one is now reduced to the situation of Lemma \ref{lem:OmeLimPerOrb}.
<!-- end rem-17 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Suppose that 
\[
{\cal O}_{x}^{+}\subseteq K\Subset U.
\]
Then $\omega(x)\subseteq K.$ Since $\omega(x)$ is nonempty, compact
and $W$-invariant, it contains a minimal compact, $W$-invariant
subset (a nonempty, compact $W$-invariant subset which contains no
proper, nontrivial invariant subsets), say $C$. Let $y\in C.$ Then
\[
\omega(y)\subseteq C\implies\omega(y)=C
\]
since $C$ is minimal. In particular, $y\in\omega(y)$. According
to Lemma \ref{lem:PRPerOrb}, ${\cal O}_{y}$ is a periodic orbit.
Hence $\omega(x)$ contains a periodic orbit. It follows from Lemma
\ref{lem:OmeLimPerOrb} that $\omega(x)=C$.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- rem-18: body_md -->
Here is a simple variant of the Poincar\'e-Bendixson theorem. Let
$W$ be a smooth, nonvanishing vector field on a compact surface $M$
without boundary. Suppose that there exists 
\[
K\ \text{compact},\quad U\ \text{open},\quad K\Subset U\subseteq M
\]
and $t_{0}\geqslant0,$ such that $U$ is diffeomorphic to a planar
domain and $\phi_{t}(x)\in K$ for all $t\geqslant t_{0}$. Then $\omega(x)$
is a periodic orbit of $W$. A similar assertion holds for $\alpha(x)$.
<!-- end rem-18 -->
<!-- lem-34: body_md -->
\label{lem:DistEndPO} Let $A\cong S^{1}\times[0,1]$ be an embedded
annulus in $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ whose two boundary curves are compact
leaves of ${\cal F}_{W}$. Let $x\in{\rm int}A$ and assume that ${\cal O}_{x}$
is nonperiodic. Then $\alpha(x)$ and $\omega(x)$ are distinct periodic
orbits.
<!-- end lem-34 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Let $U\supseteq A$ be a slightly larger open annulus which is diffeomorphic
to a planar domain. According to the Poincar\'e-Bendixson theorem,
both $\alpha(x)$ and $\omega(x)$ are periodic orbits and they are
contained in $A$. Suppose on the contrary that $\alpha(x)=\omega(x)=C.$
Let $p\in C$. Then both tails of ${\cal O}_{x}$ are arbitrarily
close to $C$. In particular, there exists $T_{0}>0$ such that $\phi_{t}(x)\in U$
for all $|t|>T_{0}.$ 

Now choose a small flow box centered at $p$ with transversal $\Sigma$.
Similar to the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:PRPerOrb}, one can find a
two-sided sequence 
\[
-\infty\downarrow s_{-n}<\cdots<s_{-2}<s_{-1}<s_{1}<s_{2}<\cdots<s_{n}\uparrow\infty
\]
with the following properties:

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) $z_{n}:=\phi_{s_{n}}(x)\in\Sigma$ and
$\phi_{t}\notin\Sigma$ for all $t\in(s_{n-1},s_{n})$ and for all
$n\in\mathbb{Z}$;

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) $z_{n}\rightarrow p$ as $n\rightarrow\pm\infty.$

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iii) The sequence $\{z_{n}\}_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}$
is monotone on $\Sigma.$

\vspace{2mm}\noindent But the second and third properties force the
sequence to be constant, which would imply that ${\cal O}_{x}$ is
periodic. This leads to a contradiction. Therefore, $\alpha(x)$ and
$\omega(x)$ are distinct periodic orbits.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- rem-19: body_md -->
Lemma \ref{lem:DistEndPO} may fail on the whole torus $\mathbb{T}^{2}$;
it is certainly possible for a nonperiodic orbit to approach the same
periodic orbit $C$ in both tails. However, if one cuts $\mathbb{T}^{2}$
along $C$ to obtain a compact annulus whose two boundary curves are
copies of $C$ (and they are considered as distinct periodic orbits),
Lemma \ref{lem:DistEndPO} is indeed applicable to this situation.
<!-- end rem-19 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:OrbitSetClose}(i) Let $A\cong S^{1}\times[0,1]$ be an
embedded annulus in $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ whose two boundary curves are
compact leaves of ${\cal F}_{W}$. Let ${\cal P}_{A}:=\{x\in A:{\cal O}_{x}\text{ is periodic}\}$.
Then ${\cal P}_{A}$ is a closed subset of $A$.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) Let ${\cal P}:=\{x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}:{\cal O}_{x}\text{ is periodic}\}$.
Then ${\cal P}$ is closed.
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
(i) Let $x_{n}\in{\cal P}_{A}$ and $x_{n}\rightarrow x$. Suppose
on the contrary that ${\cal O}_{x}$ is nonperiodic. According to
Lemma \ref{lem:DistEndPO}, 
\begin{equation}
C_{-}:=\alpha(x),\quad C_{+}:=\omega(x)\label{eq:POClosednessPf}
\end{equation}
are distinct periodic orbits on $A$. Recall from Proposition \ref{prop:POTop}
that both $C_{\pm}$ are essential, simple closed curves. As a result,
they bound a subannulus $A'$ and $x\in{\rm int}A'$. Since $x_{n}\rightarrow x,$
there is a large $n$ such that the periodic orbit ${\cal O}_{x_{n}}$
is contained inside ${\rm int}A'$, hence dividing ${\rm int}A'$
into two connected components. The point $x$ lies inside one of these
two components. In order for the orbit ${\cal O}_{x}$ to approach
$C_{\pm}$ in both tails (see (\ref{eq:POClosednessPf})), it must
cross the periodic orbit ${\cal O}_{x_{n}}$. Hence ${\cal O}_{x}\cap{\cal O}_{x_{n}}\neq\emptyset$,
which is a contradiction. Therefore, ${\cal O}_{x}$ is periodic.\begin{figure}[H] 
\begin{center}  
\includegraphics[scale=0.15]{closedness} 
\end{center}
\end{figure}\noindent (ii) Let $x_{n}\in{\cal P}$ and $x_{n}\rightarrow x$.
Suppose that $x\notin{\cal O}_{x_{1}}$; otherwise, ${\cal O}_{x}$
is periodic and there is nothing to prove. Cutting $\mathbb{T}^{2}$
along ${\cal O}_{x_{1}}$ yields a compact annulus $A$ with $x_{n}\in{\cal P}_{A}$
and $x_{n}\rightarrow x\in{\rm int}A.$ The result of Part (i) then
implies that ${\cal O}_{x}$ is periodic.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- defn-18: body_md -->
\label{def:Suspension}The foliation $(\Sigma_{f},{\cal F}_{f})$
is called the \textit{suspension} of the diffeomorphism $f$. The
vector field $\partial_{t}$ is called the \textit{suspension field}.
<!-- end defn-18 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
(i) Let $f={\rm id}_{S^{1}}$. The orbits of $\partial_{t}$ are the
vertical circles and they are all periodic with period one. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) (Rational rotation) Let $f(x):=x+p/q$
$({\rm mod\ \mathbb{Z}})$ where $p,q$ are coprime integers ($q>0$).
Then $f^{q}={\rm id}_{S^{1}}$. All orbits are periodic with period
$q$.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iii) (Irrational rotation) Let $f(x):=x+\alpha$
$({\rm mod\ \mathbb{Z}})$ where $\alpha\notin\mathbb{Q}$. Every
orbit is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$ and is dense in $\mathbb{T}^{2}$. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iv) Suppose that $f$ has precisely one fixed
point $[a]\in S^{1}$. Then $f$ can be viewed as a diffeomorphism
on $(a,a+1)$ with no fixed points. Suppose further that $f(x)>x$
for all $x\in(a,a+1)$. Then there is precisely one periodic orbit
\[
C:t\mapsto[(a,t)]
\]
which has period one. Every orbit other than $C$ is nonperiodic (hence
diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$) and approaches $C$ in both ends.
 \begin{figure}[H] 
\begin{center}  
\includegraphics[scale=0.14]{suspension_example}
\protect\caption{Suspension examples.}\label{fig:susp_exam}
\end{center}
\end{figure}\noindent (v) Suppose that $f$ has precisely two fixed points $[a],[b]\in S^{1}.$
With suitable choice of representatives, let us assume that $b\in(a,a+1)$.
Suppose that $f(x)>x$ on $(a,b)$ and $f(x)<x$ on $(b,a+1)$. Then
there are precisely two periodic orbits 
\[
C_{a}:t\mapsto[(a,t)],\quad C_{b}:t\mapsto[(b,t)].
\]
All other orbits are nonperiodic. Figure \ref{fig:susp_exam} sketches
the flow lines on the universal cover $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ for Cases
(iv) and (v).\textcolor{blue}{{} }
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- rem-20: body_md -->
\label{rem:PeriodicPt}Periodic orbits of $(\Sigma_{f},{\cal F}_{f})$
correspond to periodic points of $f$. A point $x\in S^{1}$ is a
\textit{periodic point} of $f$ if there exists a positive integer
$q$ such that $f^{q}(x)=x$. The smallest such $q$ is called the
\textit{period} of $x.$ For an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism
$f\in{\rm Diff}(S^{1})$, the period of a periodic point is intrinsic
to $f$ and does not depend on the actual point $x$.
<!-- end rem-20 -->
<!-- defn-19: body_md -->
A smooth, simple closed curve $\Sigma$ is a \textit{complete transversal}
if it intersects every orbit of $W$ transversally.
<!-- end defn-19 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:SuspChara}The foliation ${\cal F}_{W}$ is conjugate
to a suspension if and only if there exists a complete transversal.
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
(i) Necessity is obvious. In fact, the horizontal circle 
\[
S^{1}\ni t\mapsto[(t,0)]\in\Sigma_{f}
\]
is a complete transversal of the suspension foliation. It remains
to prove sufficiency. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) Let $\Sigma$ be a given complete transversal.
For each $x\in\Sigma,$ we define the first return time
\[
\tau(x):=\inf\{t>0:\phi_{t}(x)\in\Sigma\}.
\]
We first show that $\tau(x)<\infty$. Suppose on the contrary that
$\phi_{t}(x)$ never meets $\Sigma$ again at any positive time. We
claim that there exists $T_{0}>0$ and a small neighbourhood $N$
of $\Sigma,$ such that $\phi_{t}(x)\notin N$ for all $t>T_{0}$.
Indeed, if this were not the case, there would exist a sequence of
times $t_{n}\rightarrow\infty$ such that $\phi_{t_{n}}(x)$ converges
to some $y\in\Sigma$. Draw a flow box $(V;s,r)$ centered at $y=(0,0)$
so that $\Sigma\cap V=\{s=0\}$. One can write $\phi_{t_{n}}(x)=(s_{n},r_{n})$
under the flow box coordinates and note that $(s_{n},r_{n})\rightarrow(0,0)$.
Since the flow lines are precisely $s\mapsto(s,r)$ inside $V,$ one
has 
\[
\phi_{-s_{n}}\big(\phi_{t_{n}}(x)\big)=\phi_{t_{n}-s_{n}}(x)=(0,r_{n})\in\Sigma
\]
for all large $n$. As a result, the time $t_{n}-s_{n}$ is a positive
return time for large $n$ (because $t_{n}\rightarrow\infty$ and
$s_{n}\rightarrow0$) which leads to a contradiction. Therefore, $\{\phi_{t}(x):t>0\}$
is contained outside a tubular neighbourhood $N$ of $\Sigma$ after
some short period of time. Similar to the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:POTop}
(i), it can be shown that any complete transversal must be essential.
As a result, $N^{c}$ (as a compact annulus) is contained in a planar
domain. By applying the Poincar\'e-Bendixson theorem, one obtains
a periodic orbit that is disjoint from $\Sigma.$ This contradicts
the completeness of $\Sigma.$ Consequently, $\tau(x)<\infty$.

We define the first return map
\begin{equation}
Q:\Sigma\rightarrow\Sigma,\quad Q(x):=\phi_{\tau(x)}(x).\label{eq:FirstRetMapQ}
\end{equation}
By realising a neighbourhood of $Q(x)$ on $\Sigma$ as a level set
$\{\rho=0\}$ for some smooth function $\rho,$ one can apply the
same argument as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:PoinMap} (construction
of the Poincar\'e map) to conclude that $\tau(x)$ is a smooth in
$x$. Therefore, $Q\in C^{\infty}(\Sigma)$. It is indeed a diffeomorphism
since $Q^{-1}$ is defined in the same way by the return-to-$\Sigma$
map of the inverse flow $-W$. Let $\sigma:S^{1}\stackrel{\cong}{\rightarrow}\Sigma$
be an $S^{1}$-parametrisation of $\Sigma.$ Then $f:=\sigma^{1}\circ Q\circ\sigma\in{\rm Diff}(S^{1})$.
\begin{figure}[H] 
\begin{center}  
\includegraphics[scale=0.12]{suspension_pf} 
\end{center}
\end{figure}\noindent (iii) We claim that $f$ is orientation preserving, or
more precisely, $f'(r)>0$ for all $r$ (here we identify $S^{1}:=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$
so that one has the canonical isomorphisms $T_{r}S^{1}\cong T_{f(r)}S^{1}\cong\mathbb{R}$).
The argument is in spirit similar to the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:CharaNum}
(positivity of the transversal characteristic number).

To this end, let $\Omega$ be a volume form on $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ such
that 
\[
g(r):=\Omega\big(W(\sigma(r)),\dot{\sigma}(r)\big)>0
\]
for all $r\in S^{1}$. This is possible since $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ is
orientable and $\Sigma$ is transversal to $W$. Let 
\begin{equation}
F(s,r):=\phi_{s\tau(\sigma(r))}(\sigma(r))\label{eq:Fsr}
\end{equation}
and define 
\[
J(s,r):=\Omega\big(W(F(s,r)),\partial_{r}F(s,r)\big).
\]
It is plain to see that 
\begin{align}
\partial_{s}F(s,r) & =\tau(\sigma(r))W(F(s,r)),\nonumber \\
\partial_{r}F(s,r) & =(d\phi_{s\tau(\sigma(r))})\dot{\sigma}(r)+s\tau'(r)W(F(s,r)).\label{eq:DrF}
\end{align}
Since $\dot{\sigma}(r)$ and $W(\sigma(r))$ are linearly independent,
so are 
\[
(d\phi_{s\tau(\sigma(r))})\dot{\sigma}(r)\quad\text{and}\quad(d\phi_{s\tau(\sigma(r))})W(\sigma(r))=W(F(s,r)).
\]
As a result, 
\[
J(s,r)=\Omega\big(W(F(s,r)),(d\phi_{s\tau(\sigma(r))})\dot{\sigma}(r)\big)
\]
has constant sign. Note that $J(0,r)=g(r)>0$. It follows that 
\[
J(1,r)=\Omega\big(W(\sigma\circ f(r)),f'(r)\dot{\sigma}(f(r))\big)=f'(r)g(f(r))>0.
\]
Therefore, $f'(r)>0$ and $f$ is orientation preserving.

Now let $\Sigma_{f}$ be the suspension of $f$. Define $\Psi:\Sigma_{f}\rightarrow\mathbb{T}^{2}$
by 
\[
\Psi([r,t]):=\phi_{t\tau(\sigma(r))}(\sigma(r)),\quad r\in S^{1},t\in[0,1].
\]
The definition of $\Psi$ is consistent at the junction $t=0=1$ (${\rm mod}\ \mathbb{Z}$).
In addition, $\Psi$ is a homeomorphism and maps the suspension foliation
to ${\cal F}_{W}$. The issue is that $\Psi$ may fail to be a diffeomorphism.
This is because 
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\Big|_{t=1^{-}}\phi_{t\tau(\sigma(r))}(\sigma(r))\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\Big|_{t=0^{+}}\phi_{t\tau(\sigma\circ f(r))}(\sigma\circ f(r))
\]
need not coincide. They coincide precisely when $\tau(\sigma(r))=\tau(\sigma\circ f(r))$,
which needs not be true in general.

The above issue can be fixed by a simple leaf reparametrisation. Let
\[
\theta(r,t):=ct+(\tau(\sigma(r))-c)\beta(t),\quad r\in S^{1},t\in[0,1].
\]
Here 
\[
0<c<\inf_{r\in S^{1}}\tau(\sigma(r))
\]
and $\beta:[0,1]\rightarrow[0,1]$ is smooth, nondecreasing and satisfies
\[
\beta=0\text{ near }0,\quad\beta=1\text{ near }1.
\]
Then one has 
\[
\theta(r,0)=0,\quad\theta(r,1)=\tau(\sigma(r)),
\]
\[
\theta(r,t)=ct\text{ near }t=0,
\]
\[
\theta(r,t)=\tau(\sigma(r))+c(t-1)\text{ near }t=1.
\]
This ensures that all $t$-derivatives match at the junction $t=0=1$
(${\rm mod}\ \mathbb{Z}$). Now we adjust the definition of $\Psi$
to be 
\[
\hat{\Psi}:\Sigma_{f}\rightarrow\mathbb{T}^{2},\quad\hat{\Psi}([r,t]):=\phi_{\theta(r,t)}(\sigma(r)).
\]
This new map $\hat{\Psi}$ is now easily seen to be a diffeomorphism,
which provides a smooth conjugation between $\Sigma_{f}$ and $\mathbb{T}^{2}$.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- defn-20: body_md -->
We say that ${\cal F}_{W}$ \textit{contains a Reeb component} if
there exists an embedded annulus $A\cong S^{1}\times[0,1]$ inside
$\mathbb{T}^{2}$ such that the following two properties are satisfied:

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) $\partial A$ is the union of two compact
leaves that are in opposite homology classes (under the $W$-orientation);

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) there are no compact leaves of ${\cal F}_{W}$
in the interior of $A$.
<!-- end defn-20 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:ReebCrit}The foliation ${\cal F}_{W}$ has a Reeb component
if and only if there exist two periodic orbits with opposite homology
classes.
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Necessity follows immediate from the definition and Proposition \ref{prop:POTop}.
We now prove sufficiency. Let $C_{+},C_{-}$ be two periodic orbits
with opposite homology classes. Let $A$ be a compact annulus bounded
by $C_{\pm}.$ Define ${\cal P}_{A}^{\pm}$ to be the set of points
in $A$ whose orbit is homologous to $C_{\pm}.$ According to Proposition
